name: demo
diagram_type: flowchart TD (6 nodes: stadium, rect x3, diamond, circle; 2 labeled edges, 1 back-edge cycle E->B, 1 thick edge ==>)
overall_verdict: Most of flowmaid's drawing is cleaner than mermaid's: a straight spine with no jogs, a compact diamond, tidy label pills, and a smaller canvas. Two things make it look worse at a glance. The error loop E->B is drawn as a huge lasso-shaped Bezier that ends in a nearly flat arrowhead, half hidden under Read input's bottom-right corner. And the thick D==>F edge gets an arrowhead twice the normal size. The labeled rank is also cramped, because 'yes'/'no' get no extra rank height, so the branch edges shrink to small hooks around the pills. Fixing the back-edge routing and the size of the marker on thick edges would remove most of the 'ugly' impression.
flowmaid_better: Spine Start -> Read input -> Valid? is one straight centred column (all at x=163.9). Mermaid's B->C has a Z-jog (185.6 -> 154.8 via y=162) because its diamond is offset, and its C->E 'no' edge has an ugly double hook just before the arrowhead (239.8 -> 258 at y=434).
Diamond fits its text: 102x65 vs mermaid's 171x171, which takes up the middle of the mermaid drawing and pushes the whole chart to 614px tall.

Edge labels are white rounded pills (rx 4, 1px #d5d9ec border) centred exactly on the curve. Mermaid's labels are flat translucent grey rectangles (rgba(204,204,204,.5)) with no padding, which look like highlighter marks.
Node sizes fit their text (Read input 99.7, Process data 114.2) instead of mermaid's fixed 152px minimum width. The canvas is smaller overall: 383x532 vs 360x614.
Process data and Show error sit symmetrically under the diamond: (85.1+242.7)/2 = 163.9.
Labels are plain SVG <text>, not <foreignObject>/HTML, so the SVG renders the same in non-browser viewers (Inkscape, rsvg, image pipelines). Mermaid's labels disappear in those.
The semantic fills tell terminal, decision and process nodes apart at a glance. This is a deliberate choice, and mermaid's all-white nodes rely on shape alone.

verified.title: Back-edge E->B is a huge free-form arc that dominates the diagram
verified.reasoning: The SVG has the single cubic 'M 222.1 348.6 C 352.8 308.6, 355.2 204.0, 191.5 164.0'. Its apex works out to x = 0.125*(222.1+191.5) + 0.75*~354 ≈ 317.5, which is 24px past Show error's right edge (293.2). In the PNG it is the biggest stroke in the picture. Mermaid's data-points for L_E_B_0 are an orthogonal route (302,454)->(302,162)->(229.6,162)->(229.6,142) with 7px Q corners. One nuance: every flowmaid edge is a cubic, so this is not 'the only free-form curve'. It is the only large one, and the claim's substance holds.
verified.root_cause: Three things combine. (1) layout.rs:1368-1376 deliberately gives back-edges no dummy channel ('it keeps the sideways bow instead'), so lo.edge_paths is empty and scene_from_layout falls back to edge_points. (2) The back-edge branch of scene.rs edge_points (3342-3370) emits one cubic [p0, (bt, p0.y-40), (bt, p3.y+40), p3]. bt is solved so the t=0.5 apex clears ext_r of ALL layers l0..=l1 inclusive (scene.rs:3356) by 24 + label_w/2 (scene.rs:3360). Those layers include the two end nodes, so the apex has to clear Show error itself (293.2+24 = 317.2) and the controls end up at x≈354. (3) Both ends are anchored toward the other node's centre (scene.rs:3323-3324 -> anchor bias 0.35 at scene.rs:3293), not toward the bow side. router::repair (router.rs:4166+) only reroutes edges that score defects, so this clean but ugly curve is never touched.
verified.fix_sketch: Small fix, tested in a scratch copy: clear only the nodes other than the two ends, i.e. pass `layer_extents(&lo, |v| v != e.from && v != e.to)` for back-edges in scene_from_layout, and re-anchor p0/p3 toward the bow (`anchor(a, sa, (bt, a.l), off, false)`, `anchor(b, sb, (bt, b.l), off, true)`). Result: canvas 383->321 wide, apex ≈247 (inside Show error's x-range), entry about 37°. All 612 lib tests pass. The quality gate trips once (wide-labels lbl_crowd 4), so labelled back-edges need tuning, and layout.rs drawn_breadth (2123-2148) must get the same rule. Mermaid-parity fix: give back-edges orthogonal lane waypoints [p0, (p0.x, p0.y-20), (lane, ..), (lane, p3.y+20), (p3.x, p3.y+20), p3], with lane = intermediate layers' extent + 24 and corners rounded, so spline_d draws mermaid's rounded orthogonal route. A ~25-line prototype reproduced mermaid's route exactly (up from Show error, a short jog, vertical arrow into Read input) but regressed bench-75/dense-td quality ceilings, so it needs proper integration with ports/nudge.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Routes the cycle orthogonally: straight up from Show error's top at x=302, a short jog at y=162, then vertically into Read input's bottom at x=229.6. It uses rounded 7px corners like every other edge.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Draws one cubic with both control points at x≈354, swinging about 24px past Show error and about 102px right of the diamond. It reads as a lasso and widens the canvas.

verified.title: Loop arrowhead enters Read input at ~14° and is partly covered by the node
verified.reasoning: A 6x zoom of (150-240, 130-190) shows the triangle's upper flank and tip disappearing under Read input's border and fill. The final tangent (355.2,204)->(191.5,164) is atan(40/163.7) = 13.7°. The arrowhead base is 9.5px wide, so its upper corner sits about 4.6px above the line, which puts it above the border y=164. Edges are emitted before node <g>s, so the node paints over it.
verified.root_cause: scene.rs:3370 puts the second control at (bt, p3.y+40), which forces a near-horizontal approach whenever bt is far from p3.x. The marker uses orient=auto (scene.rs:2806-2808). The edge loop (scene.rs:2858+) runs before the nodes are drawn, so the rect covers whatever part of the head crosses the border.
verified.fix_sketch: Comes with the loop-lasso fix. With the small fix the entry rises to about 37° (tested), but the head still touches the border. To get it right, keep the final tangent within about 30° of the face normal, e.g. c2 = (p3.x + 0.3*(bt-p3.x), p3.y + lead), or use the orthogonal-lane variant, whose last stub enters vertically. A cheap extra safeguard: when the end tangent is more than 45° off the face normal, move the end onto the node's side face (side_point) instead of the bottom face.
verified.what_mermaid_does: The last segment (229.58,154.9)->(229.58,146) is vertical, so the arrowhead points straight up and sits clear of the box.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The arrowhead lies almost flat along the bottom border near Read input's right corner, and the node's fill and stroke cover its upper half.

verified.title: Thick edge D==>F gets an arrowhead twice the normal size
verified.reasoning: The SVG has stroke-width="3.4" with marker-end="url(#arrow)", and #arrow has markerWidth=7 and no markerUnits, so the box is 7*3.4 = 23.8px against 11.9px on the 1.7px edges. A 6x zoom shows a fat triangle. Mermaid's pointEnd-margin uses markerUnits=userSpaceOnUse at 10.5x14 for every thickness. I checked the mechanism: adding `linkStyle 5 stroke-width:3.4px` switches the edge to #arrow-u (11.9px userSpaceOnUse).
verified.root_cause: scene.rs:2494 sets `user_space: m == Marker::Arrow && st.stroke_width.is_some()`, which is true only when linkStyle sets a width. A `==>` edge gets its width from its kind (scene.rs:2865, EDGE_WIDTH_THICK = 3.4 at scene.rs:2442), so it falls back to the base #arrow def (scene.rs:2806-2808), which scales with stroke width.
verified.fix_sketch: Change it to `user_space: m == Marker::Arrow && (st.stroke_width.is_some() || matches!(e.kind, EdgeKind::Thick | EdgeKind::ThickOpen))`. id_for covers the start marker too, so <==> is handled. Tested in scratch: the head becomes 11.9px, and only 2 byte-exact marker tests fail (diagrams_without_link_style_render_exactly_as_before, edge_markers_draw_at_the_right_ends). Ship it together with the line-past-arrow-tip fix: with the smaller head, the 3.4px stroke visibly pokes out past the tip (confirmed in a zoom of the scratch render).
verified.what_mermaid_does: Marker size is fixed in user space, so the 3.5px thick edge has the same 10.5x14 head as the 2px edges.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The head scales with stroke width: a 23.8px marker box on the thick edge against 11.9px on normal edges, so it looks like a different, clumsy glyph.

verified.title: Loop leaves Show error almost tangent to its top border, crowded next to the 'no' arrowhead
verified.reasoning: In a zoom of (190-260, 320-360), the 'no' arrowhead tip at 208.1 and the loop start at 222.1 sit 14px apart. The loop leaves at atan(40/130.7) = 17° and slides up and right over the box's top-left third. Show error's right half (x>242) is empty.
verified.root_cause: The loop start is anchored toward Read input's centre: anchor(a, sa, (b.b, b.l), ...) at scene.rs:3323 with the 0.35 bias at scene.rs:3293 gives x = 242.7 - 27.6 = 215.1. That is the same point the 'no' end gets (its bias toward C is also -27.6). ports.rs respace then splits the two only by PORT_SPACING = 14 (ports.rs:23), giving 208.1 and 222.1. The departure direction comes from c1 = (bt≈352.8, p0.y-40), hence the shallow 17°.
verified.fix_sketch: Part of the loop-lasso fix: anchor the back-edge ends toward bt, which moves the start to E's right half (x≈247-281), well away from 'no', and use a steeper c1 or a vertical stub. Tested: the start moves to 247 and the 'no' end returns to 215.1 (32px apart).
verified.what_mermaid_does: The back-edge leaves Show error's top perpendicularly at x=302, 44px from where 'no' arrives (x=258).
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The loop starts 14px from the 'no' arrowhead and leaves at about 17°, so it seems to slide along the top border.

verified.title: Labeled rank gets no extra height, so 'yes'/'no' edges become tiny hooks around the pills
verified.reasoning: All four gaps between ranks are exactly 60px. The pills span y=303.6..323.6, which leaves about 25px of stroke above each pill and 25px below, and about 11px of the lower part is arrowhead (the first pass said ~15px; the effect is the same). The S-curve inflection sits under the pill, so a 4x zoom reads as '( yes )' brackets. Mermaid gives this rank about 100px.
verified.root_cause: layout.rs:1903-1911 grows a gap for a labelled edge between adjacent layers only when the label would overlap its own end nodes (`if at - ends < ext`, ext = LABEL_BOX_H = 20). Otherwise the fixed GAP_L = 60 applies (layout.rs:57). Dagre, which mermaid uses, halves ranksep, doubles minlen and turns the label into a dummy node, so labelled ranks get label height plus spacing on both sides.
verified.fix_sketch: For TD/BT only (horizontal flows already size by label width), require gap >= GAP_L + LABEL_BOX_H + 2*LABEL_CLEAR on any layer pair that carries a labelled short edge. A naive version applied to all directions (`at - ends < ext + GAP_L`) produced the expected nicer TD render (gap 80, longer stubs). It broke 2 LR gap tests and several quality ceilings because it also inflated LR, so it needs to be gated on direction and the ceilings re-baselined.
verified.what_mermaid_does: The labelled rank is about 100px deep, with long straight stubs above and below each label.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The labelled rank keeps the 60px default, so each branch is an S-curve with only about 25px showing on each side of the pill.

verified.title: Branch arrows land off-centre on their targets for no reason
verified.reasoning: The numbers are right: 'yes' ends at 112.7 against Process data's centre 85.1, and 'no' at 208.1 against Show error's 242.7. But 'for no reason' is wrong. The offset is a deliberate softening of the free-cubic style: centring 'yes' would make the S-curve shift 63px sideways in 70px of height. Mermaid can land in the centre because it routes orthogonally with a horizontal jog mid-rank. 'no' is offset further by the port split with E->B.
verified.root_cause: scene.rs:3293 anchor(): `bias = ((other.0 - p.b) * 0.35 + off).clamp(-flat, flat)` is applied at both ends, so each end leans 35% of the centre offset toward the other node. ports.rs keeps a lone end at its wanted (biased) position.
verified.fix_sketch: Put more of the lateral shift on the source end, which is the diamond flank where an angled exit looks natural, and less on the target: e.g. 0.15 at a target end that is the only end on its side. Alternatively, in ports.rs pull an end that is alone on a rect side toward the side's centre when its leg stays monotone. The real parity fix is the orthogonal edge idiom (see missed).
verified.what_mermaid_does: 'yes' lands at x=88, the exact centre of Process data.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Both branch arrows land 27-35px toward the inner corners of their targets.

verified.title: Edge stroke runs to the tip of the arrowhead and sticks out beside it
verified.reasoning: A 6x zoom of D->F shows a dark nub of full-width stroke between the triangle tip and Done's border. Geometry: the path ends on the border, and the tip sits 0.5 viewBox units beyond it (refX 8.5, tip at 9). Within about 1.6 units of the tip, the triangle's half-width (4/9 per unit) is smaller than the stroke's half-width (0.71 units). On 1.7px edges this is under 1px and practically invisible. Mermaid hides it with stroke-dasharray '0 0 <len-4> 4', leaving the last 4px unpainted, plus refX=11.5 at the tip.
verified.root_cause: Each path is emitted ending exactly at bezier[3] or the last waypoint (scene.rs:2884-2897). The marker defs put the tip only 0.5 units past the path end (scene.rs:2806-2808 and 2540-2543), so the stroke reaches the narrow part of the triangle.
verified.fix_sketch: Trim only at emission time, so router, label and casing geometry stay on the border: when an end has an arrow marker, cut the last cubic segment back by about 0.45 of the head length (de Casteljau split at the matching t) and set refX so the tip still lands on the border. Do this in the three emit paths (single cubic, spline_d, curve_d). An alternative is mermaid's dasharray trick, which needs path length. This becomes severity 2 once the thick-arrowhead fix shrinks the head relative to the 3.4px stroke (seen in the scratch render).
verified.what_mermaid_does: No stroke shows past or beside the triangle: the last 4px of the line are dashed out under the head.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The stroke runs into the narrow tip region, leaving a visible stub on the thick edge.

verified.title: Canvas width includes the arc's control points, leaving a 65px right margin
verified.reasoning: The width is 383, while the furthest drawn x is ≈317.5, a 65px margin on the right against 28px on the left. 355.2 (the control x) + 28 = 383.2, which matches exactly.
verified.root_cause: scene_from_layout adds the cubic's control points to the bbox (scene.rs:886-910, with the comment 'the control-point bbox guarantees nothing gets clipped'). grow_scene (scene.rs:3199-3201) does the same after repair. That is safe but loose, since a bow's controls reach about 33% past its apex.
verified.fix_sketch: Add a `cubic_bbox(p0,p1,p2,p3)` helper that solves the derivative quadratic per axis and adds the endpoints plus the extrema at t in (0,1). Use it in both places, keeping the hull only for curve_geometry overshoot cases. The loop-lasso fix also shrinks it here: tested width 383->321.
verified.what_mermaid_does: The viewBox hugs the drawn content with an even pad.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The canvas is padded out to the invisible Bezier control point, so the drawing looks shifted left.

verified.title: Four unrelated hues for six nodes; the two terminators get different colours
verified.reasoning: The fill and stroke values are as stated. The stadium is green and the circle violet, although both are terminators here. This is a deliberate semantic theme, but the user asked for output that looks like mermaid, and mermaid 12.2.0's default here is monochrome: white fill, #28253D 2px strokes, a drop shadow (CSS in demo.mermaid.svg).
verified.root_cause: style.rs:21-80 shape_style() hard-codes a different hue per shape, and the test every_shape_has_a_distinct_stroke (style.rs:100-113) enforces it. The flowchart writer always uses it. No neutral or mermaid theme exists.
verified.fix_sketch: Add a theme switch (an init `theme` or a CLI flag) whose default matches mermaid's neutral look: white or #ECECFF fills, one stroke ink. Keep the semantic palette as an opt-in theme. Relax or retarget the style test.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Monochrome: white fills, #28253D 2px strokes, black edges, soft drop shadow.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Green, amber, periwinkle and violet pastel fills with saturated strokes.

verified.title: Thin strokes in two different blues make the drawing look faint
verified.reasoning: Edges are 1.7px #44507a, rect and node borders are 1.6px #5b6dc0 on pale fills, and mermaid uses 2px edges in #000 and 2px node borders in #28253D. Downscaled in demo.side.png, flowmaid is clearly lighter. The arrowhead adds to this: flowmaid's triangle is about 10.7 long by 9.5 wide, against mermaid's 10.5 by 14 user-space head, so flowmaid's heads look slender as well.
verified.root_cause: EDGE_COLOR #44507a (scene.rs:50) and EDGE_WIDTH 1.7 (scene.rs:2441). The node stroke width defaults to 1.6 (scene.rs:2979) and is hard-coded at scene.rs:3037/3052/3111. Node stroke colours come from style.rs shape_style. The arrow glyph 'M 0 1 L 9 5 L 0 9 z' (scene.rs:2806-2808, 2540) is 8 units wide by 9 long.
verified.fix_sketch: With the theme work: EDGE_WIDTH 2.0, node stroke 2.0, one dark ink for edges and borders in the default theme, and a wider arrow glyph ('M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z' or a 10.5x14 userSpaceOnUse head like mermaid's). Arrow-size constants (ARROW_MARKER_PX in labels.rs/casing.rs) follow automatically. Expect snapshot and test churn.
verified.what_mermaid_does: One strong ink: 2px #28253D node borders, 2px black edges, wide 14px arrowheads.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: 1.7px slate edges and 1.6px periwinkle borders with narrow 9.5px heads, which look faint when scaled down.

missed: Edge idiom mismatch, the biggest gap for the user's 'look like mermaid' goal. In mermaid 12.2.0 every edge is an axis-aligned polyline with about 7px rounded corners: fixCorners plus curveBasis, visible in every data-points list in demo.mermaid.svg, e.g. B->C (185.6,142)->(185.6,162)->(154.8,162)->(154.8,182). In flowmaid every unrouted edge is one free cubic: edge_points at scene.rs:3306-3379 for forward edges uses [p0,(p0.x,p0.y+dl),(p3.x,p3.y-dl),p3]. The pieces for the mermaid look already exist: spline_d at scene.rs:3738 is d3 curveBasis, and the router's corner smoothing gives rounded corners. My lane prototype for the back-edge produced mermaid's exact look. A default orthogonal mode (horizontal jog at mid-rank for offset edges) would remove the S-hooks, the off-centre landings and the lasso together. Effort L.

Fixes are coupled. The thick-arrowhead fix (scene.rs:2494) makes the line-past-tip stub worse: in a scratch render with a userSpaceOnUse head, the 3.4px stroke clearly sticks out beyond the 11.9px triangle tip. The two must ship together.

Latent bug from the same root cause as the doubled head: labels.rs:92/903/913 (head keep-out boxes) and casing.rs:40/262 (MASK_PAD, head proximity) size arrowheads with the constant ARROW_MARKER_PX = 11.9px. A `==>` edge without linkStyle actually draws a 23.8px head, so label placement and casing masks under-reserve around thick arrowheads. A label can land on a thick edge's head without the quality metrics noticing. Not visible in demo; it goes away with the thick-marker fix.

The layout and scene bow rules are duplicated. layout.rs drawn_breadth (2099-2150, BOW_CLEAR = 24 at layout.rs:126, inclusive layers l0..=l1) mirrors scene.rs edge_points' bow rule, so any back-edge fix has to change both, or the layout reserves breadth the scene no longer uses (or the reverse). In scratch, changing only the scene side passed the lib tests but tripped the quality gate (wide-labels lbl_crowd = 4; the intermediate-layers-only variant gave bench-75 defects 16 > 15).

name: advanced
diagram_type: flowchart TD (nested subgraphs, edges to subgraphs, mixed shapes, thick/dotted/invisible links, classDef/style)
overall_verdict: On their own, flowmaid's nodes, labels and palette look cleaner than mermaid's. For this diagram the overall result is still worse, for two reasons. First, it silently drops the nested "Async Workers" subgraph. Second, it ignores the `Reg --> Platform` ranking constraint, so the CI/CD Pipeline cluster sits to the right of Production Platform instead of above it. That breaks the top-down story: the start node is in the top-right corner, and the hand-off into Platform goes right-to-left into the side of the frame. On top of that come several edges that bulge out of their own clusters, an oversized thick-edge arrowhead, and small S-wobbles on edges that should be straight. Together these give the "still ugly" feeling, even though each shape is nicer than mermaid's.
flowmaid_better: The W1 --> W1 self-loop is a clear loop with an arrowhead, drawn in the 50px gap between Worker 1 and Worker 2 (path M 130.9 343.5 C 178.9 323.5 ...). Mermaid's self-loop is broken: only a tiny arrow stub to the left of Worker 1, with no visible loop.

Rollback --> Platform is one short straight edge (x=295.4, from y=679 to 515.5). Mermaid sends it around the entire right side of the diagram (x≈1207) and into the top of Platform, the longest and ugliest edge in its render.
Node sizes are compact and well proportioned. Mermaid's hexagons are huge (Security scan ≈290×150, Healthy? ≈270×120 at 1x); flowmaid's are 111×55 and 115×38.
The canvas is far more compact: 807×756 versus mermaid's 906×1484. Mermaid's render is a very tall strip.
Edge labels are clean white rounded chips with a light border (rx=4, stroke #d5d9ec). Mermaid uses flat grey hsl(0,0%,80%) boxes with almost no padding.
Worker 1 and Worker 2 keep source order, left to right. Mermaid swaps them (Worker 2 | Worker 1).
Nothing overlaps a cluster title. In mermaid the thick Gate ==> Q edge runs straight through the 'Async Workers' title text.
Platform --> Healthy? is a clean straight drop. Mermaid's has a small jog/kink just below the Platform frame.
The custom classDef/style colours (human, danger, Done) are kept, and the semantic shape colouring (cylinders blue, hexagons purple) helps scanning without hurting contrast.

verified.title: Nested 'Async Workers' subgraph is not drawn
verified.reasoning: The SVG has only 2 cluster rects and no 'Async Workers' text. I reproduced it with m1.mmd (`subgraph P{subgraph Wk{Q-->W1} G-->Q; W1-->U}`), which gives 1 rect. Without the parent re-mentions (m2.mmd) it gives 2 rects. Deleting line 26 or line 27 of advanced.mmd brings the box back. Mermaid's flowDb.addSubGraph/makeUniq (chunk-NQOKRVIF.mjs:650,842) adds a subgraph when it closes and drops nodes that already belong to an earlier-added subgraph, so the first subgraph to close wins. flowmaid does the opposite: the last mention inside any block wins. I prototyped the fix in a scratch copy: Async Workers is drawn, and all 620 tests still pass.
verified.root_cause: /home/user/flowmaid/src/parser.rs:2613-2624. `if let Some(&owner) = subs.last()` removes the node from every subgraph and pushes it into the current block. `Gate ==> Q` and `W1 & W2 --> Users` come after Workers' `end` but are still inside Platform, so they pull Q, W1 and W2 back into Platform. Workers is left empty, and cluster_raw_boxes (scene.rs:2324 `if !bb.0.is_finite() { continue }`) skips it. The render.rs:191 advanced_showcase test only checks the subgraph count, the parent and the direction, never Workers.nodes.
verified.fix_sketch: In parser.rs before re-claiming: `let cur = g.subgraphs.iter().position(|s| s.nodes.contains(&n)); let closed = cur.is_some_and(|c| !subs.contains(&c)); if !closed && !g.subgraphs[owner].nodes.contains(&n) { ... }`. A node owned by an already-closed subgraph stays there; an open ancestor's claim is overridden by the inner block. Prototyped at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/rv_adv_skeptic/fm. Also add `assert_eq!(workers.nodes.len(), 3)` to the render.rs showcase test.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Orange 'Async Workers' box inside Platform around Job Queue, Worker 1 and Worker 2.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: No frame or title; the three nodes sit loose in Platform.

verified.title: Reg --> Platform (and Rollback --> Platform) have no effect on ranking, so the clusters sit side by side
verified.reasoning: Deleting line 13 changes only that edge's <path>. The first pass's cause ('combination of back-edges') was vague. The real trigger is a cycle inside the TARGET box. Deleting `Cache --> Gate` (line 18) makes the clusters stack (CI y=28..507, Platform y=539..984). Minimal check: A{a1->a2}, a2-->B, B{b1->b2} stacks (m4.mmd), but adding `b2-->b1` puts them side by side (m3.mmd). With the fallback below prototyped (plus the nested fix), CI stacks above Platform, Reg->Platform becomes a straight 46px vertical drop, the canvas is 619x1267, and all 620 tests pass. The rendered result is at rv_adv_skeptic/fix2.png.
verified.root_cause: /home/user/flowmaid/src/scene.rs:1547-1583 sub_edge_proxies. A box as edge TARGET stands for its 'entry members', meaning members with no internal in-edge (`members` closure at 1570). Every Platform member has one: Gate gets Cache->Gate, Auth/Cache/Q get edges from Gate, Users from Auth/W1/W2, W1/W2 from Q. So the proxy set is empty. The rank group is therefore empty, and scene.rs:1034 (`to.iter().find(..)` returns None) creates no stand-in edge either. Reg->Platform and Rollback->Platform end up with zero layout influence, both clusters start at rank 0, and they are placed side by side.
verified.fix_sketch: In `members`, when the filtered set is empty, fall back to the first declared member of the box (mermaid's findNonClusterChild anchor). I prototyped this as a 6-line change. A more principled version runs a DFS over the box's internal edges in declaration order and ignores DFS back-edges when filling has_in/has_out, so Gate (in-edge only from the back-edge Cache->Gate) counts as the entry. Add regression tests for m3.mmd and the showcase (assert CI.bottom < Platform.top).
verified.what_mermaid_does: CI/CD Pipeline on top, Production Platform below, then Healthy?/Live/Rollback.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Both clusters share rank band 0..3: CI at x=557..717 to the right of Platform. Developer sits in the top-right corner.

verified.title: Reg --> Platform leaves the cylinder's rim corner and enters Platform's side

name: subgraph
diagram_type: flowchart TD with nested subgraphs (subgraph inside subgraph, per-block direction LR that both renderers correctly override because of external links, cross-cluster edges, one style directive)
overall_verdict: For this diagram flowmaid is not broken. It draws all 8 nodes, 8 edges and both clusters, applies the Client style, and keeps the TD layout just as mermaid does (the inner direction LR is overridden because the subgraph has outside links). It also handles cluster titles better than mermaid. It looks less polished for four reasons. Whitespace runs vertically with no rhythm: an extra 26px of dead space sits under the first row of every cluster. The spine nodes are small, content-sized boxes of different widths, where mermaid 12 uses even 152px blocks. The two nested clusters look the same, so you can't see the nesting. Fan-out and fan-in edges land off-centre on the consumer boxes. The overall picture is taller, thinner and sparser than mermaid's (382x786, aspect 2.06, versus 466x749, aspect 1.61), even though flowmaid's nodes are smaller.
flowmaid_better: Cluster titles ('Platform', 'Event bus') sit top-left in a chip (12px bold #6a7086 on its own rect) and no edge ever crosses them. In mermaid, the GW->Auth edge strikes through 'Platform' and the Users->Bus edge strikes through 'Event bus', because mermaid centres the labels at x=237, the same x as the spine edges.

The palette is calm and fits together: tinted node fills (#eef1fb on #5b6dc0), dark-slate edges (#44507a) and soft rounded frames (rx=8). Mermaid's black 2px lines and saturated pink/teal frames look harsher.
No drop-shadow offsets. Mermaid's 4px flat shadows add visual noise and make boxes look doubled at the edges.
The canvas is narrower (382 vs 466 wide) because nodes are sized to their content instead of mermaid 12's fixed 120px minimum label width.

The SVG is portable and small: 4.3 KB of plain <text> versus 38.6 KB of mermaid output that relies on <foreignObject>/HTML. Flowmaid's renders in any SVG viewer or rasteriser. It also has role=img, aria-label and per-node/per-edge <title> tooltips.
The two Warehouse inbound arrowheads are symmetric (x=162.9 and 218.9 around centre 190.9) and clearly apart, as good as mermaid.
Semantics match mermaid. Flowmaid also ignores 'direction LR' for a subgraph that has external links, so the layout topology is the same.

verified.title: Extra 26px of empty space under the first row of each cluster gives uneven vertical rhythm
verified.reasoning: The SVG geometry matches the claim exactly. Auth 250..288 to User DB 374 is 86px, Broker 498..536 to Consumers 622 is 86px, while Client to GW and Consumers to Warehouse are 60px. I patched a scratch copy so the slot grows only on the title side. Height went from exactly 786 to 734, Auth to User DB and Broker to Consumers dropped to 60px, and the frame-crossing gaps stayed at 86px. The render looks clearly tighter. One overstatement: mermaid's own gaps are not even either (40/98/24/82/60/108px), so 'mermaid has rhythm' is generous. The real defect is that plain chained nodes inside a cluster sit farther apart (86) than nodes outside it (60), and that part holds.
verified.root_cause: src/layout.rs:1486-1496: for every real node on its cluster's top layer, `lextra[v] = extra * 2.0` (extra = CLUSTER_HEADER 26, layout.rs:71). Then layout.rs:1879-1882 sets lh = alsize + lextra, and layout.rs:1919 sets `lcoord[li] = cursor + lh / 2.0`. That centres the node in a slot of 38+52=90px, so the header's worth of room lands both above the node, where the title strip is, and below it, where nothing is. The doc comment says the slot grows 'by a header's worth', but the code doubles it to make up for centring.
verified.fix_sketch: Make the slot asymmetric. Store a signed extra (TD: on the low side; BT: on the high side). Per layer compute h_lo = max(alsize/2 + top_extra) and h_hi = max(alsize/2 + bottom_extra). Set lcoord = cursor + h_lo and advance the cursor by h_lo + h_hi + GAP_L. Switch the frame-reach check (l.1884), the short-label check (l.1906-1910) and the gap_need check (l.1913, prev_lh/2 becomes prev_hi) to h_lo/h_hi. I prototyped exactly this in a scratch copy: lib tests pass 612/612, but tests/quality.rs fails 4 gates on dense-td (min_edge_gap 1.78 < floor 12.1, edge_frame_pairs 40 > 28, defects 52 > 42, routed edge_node_x 4 > 0). Something downstream (channel/router spacing) relies on the spare 26px below the cluster-top layer, and that has to be found and given room explicitly, e.g. keep the bottom extra only on layers that carry edge dummies or labels.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Mermaid adds rank room only where a border or title sits. Auth to Users inside Platform is 24px.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Flowmaid adds the 26px title-strip room both above and below every cluster-top node, so chained nodes inside a cluster are 86px apart, against 60px outside.

verified.title: Small nodes in a lot of whitespace make the diagram tall, thin and sparse
verified.reasoning: The numbers are right. Viewboxes are 382x786 vs 466x749. Node area is 9.8% vs 15.9% of the canvas, and the aspect ratio is 2.06 vs 1.61. But this is not a separate defect. It adds up four causes: (1) the doubled title slot (issue 1), which by itself accounts for flowmaid being taller than mermaid (with the fix the height is 734 < 749); (2) GAP_L=60, which is larger than mermaid's visible plain-rank gap (Client to GW is 40px in mermaid), even though the code comment claims to mirror mermaid's ~50; (3) BASE_H=38 vs mermaid's 45/51; (4) content-sized widths (issue 3). Count it once, not on top of 1 and 3.
verified.root_cause: src/layout.rs:57 `GAP_L = 60.0` (the comment at l.53-56 says it follows mermaid's rankSpacing≈50); layout.rs:50 `BASE_H = 38.0`; layout.rs:52 `MIN_W = 54.0`; plus the doubling at layout.rs:1495.
verified.fix_sketch: Fix issue 1 first, which saves 52px. Then consider GAP_L 60→50 and BASE_H 38→42-44 (with matching LINE_H/padding), and MIN_W per issue 3. Each is a constant change, but each one moves every snapshot and the quality-gate ceilings, so budget time to re-baseline tests/quality.rs.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Mermaid 12 uses 152x45 blocks (GW 150x51) on a 466x749 canvas. Node coverage is about 16% and the aspect is 1.61.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Flowmaid uses 38px-tall nodes, 68-113px wide, with 60/86px rank gaps on a 382x786 canvas. Node coverage is about 10% and the aspect is 2.06.

Apply it to the other shapes the same way (stadium +12, hexagon +28, ...), in both layout.rs:390-405 and advance.rs:3100-3110. Then fix the two unit tests and re-baseline quality ceilings and snapshots. Optional: expose it as a config option.

(b) Make the tie-break in ports::port_order (src/ports.rs:331-336, currently 'outgoing before incoming') pair-aware, so two opposite edges between the same nodes get non-crossing, mirrored ports on facing sides. The 'ok' edge rises 60.7px over an 81px run, and SVC→DB rises 29.7 over 77 with a 3.4px stroke. Mermaid's neo look uses rounded elbows (radius about 5–7) with straight horizontal entries. The first pass praised the cubic style.

Parallel offsets are silently cancelled on LR boxes. anchor() (src/scene.rs:3288-3293) clamps the bias to flat = bsize/2 - 12 = 7px for 38px-tall nodes, so PARALLEL_GAP ±8 for the SVC/CACHE pair yields identical anchors. ports::port_order's 'outgoing before incoming' tie-break (src/ports.rs:331-336) then gives a 2-cycle crossing port orders. In a prototype that removes the hairpin, the pair crossed, and the router replaced the return edge with an orthogonal jog that mixed edge styles. Any fix for the hairpin needs this too.

Corner-hugging ends on Service Layer's right side. Three ends at PORT_SPACING 14 on a 38px side put the thick SVC→DB exit 5px from the top corner (y=83.7, top 78.7; with a 3.4px stroke the line almost touches the corner) and the back-edge arrival 5px from the bottom corner. Arrowhead tips overshoot the path end. The marker uses refX=8.5 but the glyph tip is at x=9, so every tip pokes 0.5 viewBox units past the border point: 0.6px on normal edges, 1.2px on the thick edge, where the tip visibly overlaps Database's border stroke. Fix: set refX to 9 (or 9 minus half the target's stroke width).

For I->J, the path ends at 1472.9 and the marker tip (refX 8.5 against a tip at 9, at 1.19px per unit) reaches 1473.5. The Parallelogram's left side at y=84.8 is (1486.9+1472.9)/2=1479.9, so the head floats 6.4px short. J->K starts at 1616.7, but the right side at mid-height is 1609.7, a 7px gap. J->K ends at 1676.7 (tip 1677.3) while Reverse's left side is at 1683.7, a 6.4px gap. Mermaid hits the outline exactly: I->J's data-points end at 1750.33, the midpoint of (1741.33, 1759.33). verified.root_cause: src/scene.rs:3274-3302 anchor(): only Diamond, Circle, DoubleCircle and StateStart/StateEnd go to the exact border() intersection. Every other shape takes the boxy branch (3287-3300), which returns (p.b + bias, p.l ± p.lsize/2), a point on the bounding-box side. border() itself (scene.rs:3693-3724) also approximates every other shape as a rectangle (3708). When a side holds two or more ends, ports::assign re-places them with ports.rs:189-242 span(). That function only knows Profile::Flat, Round and Diamond (ports.rs:66-88), so parallelogram and hexagon sides get Profile::Flat at the bbox line; that is why the hexagon fan-in ports sit at x=157.8 spaced 14px apart. router.rs:2961-2971 flat_shape() calls these sides straight, so the nudge slides ports along the bbox line. router.rs:417-431 outline_gap and quality.rs:470-485 treat these shapes as rectangles, so neither the router score nor the quality metrics can see the gap.
verified.fix_sketch: Add one screen-space helper beside border(): outline_n(node, side, t) -> normal coordinate. For Parallelogram and ParallelogramAlt on the Left/Right sides it interpolates linearly between the top and bottom corner x (k = min(14, w/4), as scene.rs:3068 draws it). For Hexagon on the Left/Right sides it uses the V profile x = l + k*|y-cy|/(h/2). For Cylinder on Top/Bottom it uses the cap ellipse y = ty ∓ ry*sqrt(1-(dx/rx)^2). (1) Add a final snap_ends stage in edgepass::finish_fixed right after router::nudge (edgepass.rs:308). For every drawn end on such a node it moves bezier[0]/bezier[3] (and the first/last waypoint) along the side normal onto outline_n, and shifts the adjacent control point by the same delta so the tangent is kept. The stage is idempotent. (2) Add a Profile variant built on outline_n in ports.rs span(), so spread ports land on the outline. (3) Make flat_shape() return false for these shapes' slanted sides, and teach outline_gap and quality.rs to use the true outline so the regression metrics catch this. Step (1) alone removes every visible gap.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Anchors the edge at the bounding-box side, which is up to k/2 (7px) away from the slanted side at mid-height, and up to about 10px for off-centre ports on a hexagon.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Intersects the edge with the real polygon outline, so the arrowheads touch the slanted sides.

EDGE_WIDTH = 1.7 is at scene.rs:2441.

verified.what_mermaid_does: A fixed 10.5x12.8px solid head in userSpaceOnUse units.

verified.reasoning: The facts hold. PAD_X is 16 (not 14) and MIN_W 54, so widths range from 83.6 to 143.8, and GAP_L = 60 gives 60px edges. Mermaid 12.2's neo look gets its uniform 150-156px widths from a node minWidth on the label (labelHelper: minLabelWidth = node.minWidth, and every label here is translate(-60) = 120px wide), with edges of about 40px. verified.what_mermaid_does: A 120px minimum label width (neo look), giving near-uniform ~150px nodes and ~40px edges.

missed: Fan-in/fan-out on a hexagon or parallelogram in LR leaves arrowheads floating about 10px in the air. This is the same root cause as parallelogram-edge-gap, but much more visible, and it contradicts the first pass's claim that edges land exactly on the hexagon tips. Repro: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/rv_shapes/hex.mmd (A,B,C --> H{{Hexagon}} --> P[/Para/], Q[\Rev\], R[(Db)]), rendered PNG next to it. A->H ends at (157.8,121.0) but the hexagon's left side at y=121 is x=168.1. H->P starts at (273.5,121.0) but the right side there is 263.2. H->P ends at (333.5,54.0) but Para's left side at y=54 is 337.9. Mechanism: ports.rs:189-242 span() gives Profile::Flat at the bbox, plus the scene.rs:3287-3300 boxy anchor.

`classDef default` is silently ignored, though mermaid applies it to every node without a class. It is the standard way to restyle all nodes, for example to get mermaid's white fill and dark stroke. Repro: 'flowchart LR / classDef default fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px / A[x] --> B[y]' still emits fill=#eef1fb stroke=#5b6dc0 stroke-width=1.6, while a named class (A:::k) works. Root cause: parser.rs:1985-1989 applies class_defs only to explicit `class` or `:::` assigns. Fix (S): before the assigns loop, apply class_defs.get("default") to every node that has no assigned class.

There is no theme support, so the user cannot make the output look like mermaid's. %%{init: {"theme":"neutral"}}%% and frontmatter themes are ignored (amber #d99114 strokes are still emitted), and SvgOptions (scene.rs:3791-3806) has no theme field; issue #57 is mentioned in its doc. Combined with the ignored `classDef default`, the hard-coded semantic palette in style.rs:20-80 is the only possible look. This is the main lever on the user's complaint that flowmaid looks worse.

Thick `==>` edges get a doubled arrowhead, about 21px long and 19px wide. #arrow uses strokeWidth marker units (markerWidth 7 × 3.4), see scene.rs:2806-2808 and ARROW_MARKER_UNITS at 2447. Mermaid keeps a fixed userSpaceOnUse head. Repro: 'flowchart LR / A ==> B' emits stroke-width='3.4' with marker-end url(#arrow) and markerWidth=7.

The cylinder lid arc and the subroutine's inner bars ignore a custom stroke-width. With 'style A stroke-width:4px' the body has stroke-width='4' but the lid arc and both subroutine bars stay at '1.6', because they are hard-coded at scene.rs:3037, 3052-3053 (and StateEnd at 3111). advance.rs correctly uses `sw`. Fix (S): use the resolved stroke width.

In TD, edges entering a cylinder's top off-centre stop at the bbox top, above the elliptical lid, floating about 1-2.5px. In /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/rv_shapes/td.svg, D->C ends at y=224.0 while the lid at x=197.6 is at y=226.4. Mermaid's cylinder intersect corrects for the cap. The outline_n snap proposed for parallelogram-edge-gap fixes this too.

The quality metrics and the router treat parallelograms, hexagons and cylinders as rectangles (quality.rs:470-485, router.rs:417-431 outline_gap, router.rs:2961-2971 flat_shape). The regression suite therefore cannot detect floating endpoints on these shapes, which is likely why the bug survived. Every shape fix also has to be made twice, because advance.rs (about 5520-5640) duplicates scene.rs's shape painting.

name: stress
diagram_type: flowchart TD (parallel edges, self-loop, back-edge cycle, thick cross-layer edge)
overall_verdict: Taken element by element, flowmaid's nodes, colours, label pills and compactness look nicer than mermaid's. The whole diagram reads worse because of the edge routing. Semantic fills: the decision is amber (#fcf2da/#d99114) and the process nodes are blue (#eef1fb/#5b6dc0), so node types stand out at a glance. Text contrast is good (#232840). Mermaid's default here is plain white boxes with black strokes and drop shadows.
The 'no' label sits near the decision it belongs to (pill centred at 143.7,205.4, about t≈0.17 along the curve). Mermaid puts 'no' halfway up a long dotted line, far from Check.
Crisp 1.6px node borders with rx=3 and no offset drop shadows.

verified.title: The thick A==>D edge runs through the apex of B's self-loop
verified.reasoning: An 8x zoom of x110-200, y100-200 shows the 3.4px thick stroke crossing the loop at its turning point (162,145), leaving a knot and no crossing gap. The loop path is 'M126 137 C174 117,174 173,126 153', apex x=126+0.75*48=162. The thick spline is at x≈161-162 at y=145-150. I instrumented a copy of edgepass::finish (scratchpad/stressdbg) to dump each stage. This geometry comes straight from the builder: ports, repair and nudge leave both edges alone.
verified.root_cause: There are four compounding causes. (1) src/scene.rs:3679-3688 loop_points always draws the loop on the node's RIGHT with a fixed 48px control reach (apex 36px out) and never checks which side is free. Process 1's left side is empty. (2) src/layout.rs:1350 skips self-loops, and pair_sep (src/layout.rs:2987-3025, absize/2+base+absize/2) reserves no breadth for them. The A→D dummy therefore lands at x=171.3, so the gap from B's right edge (126) to the dummy's left edge is only 37.3px. (3) src/scene.rs:3738 spline_d is a curveBasis B-spline that only approximates the channel point, so the drawn curve cuts about 9px inside it (x≈162 at y≈150 against waypoint 171.3,145). (4) Self-loops are invisible to the repair stages. edgepass.rs ctx sets drawn=false for self-loops (lines ~196-199) and router.rs:4013 info_of returns None for a==b, so a loop is never an obstacle and never triggers a reroute. casing sees only a tangential touch, so no gap is cut either.
verified.fix_sketch: In pair_sep, add loop room (0.75*ext + NODE_SEP ≈ 48px) on the side where the loop is drawn when u (or v) has a self-loop. Better, let loop_points choose the side with free room and reserve room on that side only. I tested this in a copy: adding 48px after a looped node moves the channel to x=193.6 and clears the loop. Also add each loop's bounding box to the router World as a blocked rect so later collisions get repaired. This must land together with the back-edge side fix: with only the room fix, the dashed bow (apex 191.7) and the thick channel run within about 2px of each other.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Puts the loop on Process 1's left side, away from the thick lane at x≈261.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Draws the loop on the right with no room reserved, directly in the A→D channel.

verified.title: The 'parallel' label sits on the unlabelled A→B edge
verified.reasoning: In the zoom the left (unlabelled) stroke disappears under the pill, while the labelled edge only grazes the pill's right border and cuts its bottom-right corner (x≈99.9 at y=108.9, pill right edge 100.4). The stage dump shows the builder put the label ON e1 at (104.3,96), ports moved it to (100.6,96), and labels::relabel then moved it to (70.3,98.9).
verified.root_cause: src/labels.rs:1159-1161 reads_own accepts a box when `other2 >= own2`. The new box touches both its own line (bottom-right corner, own2=0) and the sibling (other2=0), so the 0==0 tie passes even though the sibling runs through the middle of the box. At the old on-line spot the box crossed two strokes: e0, plus the thick e6 at its top-right corner within STROKE_PAD=3 (labels.rs:80). beside_line (labels.rs:1924-1932) takes a beside spot that crosses one fewer stroke, so the spot covering only the sibling won. Underneath this, parallel lanes are only PARALLEL_GAP=16 (scene.rs:35) or PORT_SPACING=14 (ports.rs:23) apart, which leaves no room for a 60px label. Mermaid/dagre give the label a dummy node, which spreads the lanes about 44px apart.
verified.fix_sketch: (a) In reads_own, measure from the box centre, or require own2 < other2 strictly; when both are 0, require the own line to pass nearer the centre. I tested the strict version: the label goes back onto its own line, which is less wrong but still covers both strokes. (b) The real fix: when a parallel group contains a labelled edge, widen that edge's offset in parallel_offsets and the port spacing to ≥ label_w/2 + STROKE_PAD + EDGE_SEP. Alternatively, prefer the beside spot on the side away from the siblings.

verified.what_flowmaid_does: Uses lanes 15px apart and puts the pill over the sibling.

verified.title: The dashed back-edge bows outside the thick channel and crosses it
verified.reasoning: The dashed curve reaches x=191.7 at its widest (sampled), outside the thick channel at about 171, and crosses it at the masked point (168.6,186.5). The crossing is avoidable within flowmaid's current layout. I forced the bow to the left in a copy, changing nothing else: the result had zero crossings, the mask disappeared and the port order stayed consistent.
verified.root_cause: src/scene.rs:3349-3370 (edge_points back-edge branch). The bow is placed from layer extents built by layer_extents(&lo, |_| true) (scene.rs:780, 750-770), which uses real nodes only. Long-edge dummies (lo.edge_paths) and self-loops are ignored. The side is then picked purely by distance at scene.rs:3365: bt_r-mid=130.9 against mid-bt_l=138.4, so right wins by 7.5px. Crossings with the A→D channel are never counted. Back-edges are never part of crossing minimisation (layout.rs treats them as cycle breakers with no dummy chain), unlike dagre, which reverses them into layered edges.
verified.fix_sketch: Cheap fix: for each candidate side, count crossings against the channel polylines of long edges and the self-loop boxes on the layers spanned, pick the side with fewer crossings, and use distance only to break ties. Also fold channel points into the extents on the chosen side (S-M). Proper fix (dagre-style): reverse back-edges into the layering so they get their own dummy lane, ordered by crossing minimisation (L).
verified.what_mermaid_does: Runs the dotted lane between the node column and the thick lane, with zero crossings.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Bows right past the thick channel, which forces one crossing whose gap is hidden by the dash pattern.

name: fanout
diagram_type: flowchart TD (fan-out/fan-in with a labelled decision loop-back)
overall_verdict: Flowmaid's nodes, colours, label chips and overall composition look better than mermaid's here. The layout is compact and symmetric, and the diamond and stadium are well proportioned. What makes it look worse is the edge routing. The "no" loop-back cuts through the middle of the diagram, crosses two fan-in edges, and leaves gap cuts that read as broken lines. Smooth Bezier curves are mixed with one orthogonal polyline, the outer Worker edges attach off-centre, and two edges that should be straight have small kinks. Mermaid's routing has no crossings and uses one consistent style, even though its layout is lopsided. That is why mermaid looks tidier, even though flowmaid's individual elements are nicer.
flowmaid_better: Balanced composition: every rank is centred on one vertical spine at x=350.2. Mermaid shifts the diamond and Done right (x=726, while Aggregator is at x=472 and Dispatcher at x=568), which leaves a large empty lower-left quadrant.
Much more compact: 700x513 against mermaid's 991.6x648 (about 44% less area), with even 60px gaps between ranks. Mermaid's rank gaps are uneven: 76/56/40/97px.

The decision diamond is 192x64.6 and fits its one line of text. Mermaid draws a 171x171 square diamond that wastes about 100px of height. Done is a 77x38 stadium, while mermaid's terminal is as wide as its huge diamond.

Edge labels are white rounded chips (rx=4, 1px #d5d9ec border, 20px tall) and look deliberate. Mermaid's labels sit on a 50%-opacity grey hsl(0,0%,80%) box with no padding (foreignObject 15.6x21 for 'no'), which looks unfinished.

Semantic fills add hierarchy without hurting contrast: process nodes are #eef1fb/#5b6dc0, the decision is amber #fcf2da/#d99114, the terminal is green #e5f5ea/#33a35c, and text is #232840. Mermaid's neo look is all white boxes with black 2px strokes and faint drop shadows.
Node boxes are tighter (88.9x38, against mermaid's 152x45), so the 5 workers fit in 644px instead of about 920px.
Leaner, more portable SVG: 6.2KB with plain <text> elements, against 86KB of mermaid output with foreignObject labels that fail in many non-browser renderers.

verified.title: The 'no' loop-back edge runs through the middle of the diagram instead of around it
verified.reasoning: The SVG matches the claim. 'D -> A: no' climbs x=286.8 from y≈305 to y≈116, then jogs along y=113.5 from x=289 to x=334 and rises at x=338.5 into Dispatcher's bottom. Clearances are exactly the router minimum: 299.3-286.8 = 12.5 from Aggregator, and 126-113.5 = 12.5 above Worker 3, which the jog passes over for about 28px. It crosses B2->C at (286.8,195.7) and B1->C at (286.8,209.4). It enters the bottom between A->B2 (x=324.5) and A->B3 (x=352.5), 14px from each, and runs alongside them for about 47px. Mermaid's L_D_A_0 data-points decode to 751→980 (y=307), 980 up to y=77, then left to x=615, with no crossings. I traced the pipeline with debug prints in a private copy (scratchpad/fm_fanout_rev). The builder first drew a cubic bow round the LEFT side, controls at builder x≈30 and endpoints at x≈500. Sampling that bow shows its return leg cutting Worker 1's box at t≈0.675–0.70, at (189–201, 131–139) against Worker 1 at 187..276 × 126..164. That node hit triggers router::repair. The router's first try searches only the stubs' bbox grown by ROUTE_WINDOW=160, which excludes both outer corridors. It found the interior path, which hits no node and overlaps nothing, so it was accepted at once. Crossings are only priced, not counted as hard faults. Two experiments confirm this. A whole-drawing window alone (FMWIN) gives the same interior path. CROSS_COST=400 alone, still windowed, exits the left vertex but still crosses A->B1 and B1->C. A whole-drawing window plus CROSS_COST=400 plus H_WEIGHT=1.0 gives a clean outer loop with zero crossings: left vertex → left → up → Dispatcher's left side (fanrev/w_c400_h1.png).
verified.root_cause: There are two stacked causes. (1) Bow: /home/user/flowmaid/src/scene.rs:3349-3368, the back-edge branch of edge_points(). Its controls (bt, p0.1-40) and (bt, p3.1+40) are solved so that only the apex x(0.5) clears lay_ext; nothing checks the rest of the curve. Here the return leg sweeps diagonally across Worker 1's corner. bow_blocked() at scene.rs:719 exists but is only used on the clustered path (scene.rs:806-845). (2) Reroute: /home/user/flowmaid/src/router.rs:4361-4367. The first Try uses reach: ROUTE_WINDOW (router.rs:218, 160px), so the outer corridors are not in the lattice. At router.rs:4437-4441 a candidate that is clean (no node/frame/chip hits, router.rs:476) and lone (no overlap) is taken immediately ('decided = true; break'), whatever its s.cross. CROSS_COST=120 (router.rs:129, applied in price_seg at router.rs:2059/2069) means 2 crossings (240) cost less than the extra length of an outer path, even with a full window. H_WEIGHT=1.5 (router.rs:227/2389) adds a stair jog to the outer path when one is found. The comment in layout.rs:1365-1372 shows back edges get no channel dummies on purpose, so the layout reserves no outer lane.
verified.fix_sketch: In router::repair, for an edge with cx.back[i] in Mode::Static: (a) run the first try with reach=f64::INFINITY; (b) multiply the crossing price for that edge's lattice by about 3–4×, e.g. pass a cross factor into Lattice::build/price_seg; (c) do not 'decide' on a candidate with s.cross>0. Instead keep the best candidate and let the wider/walls tries look for a zero-crossing one. (d) Use H_WEIGHT=1.0 for that search, or run merge_jog afterwards. The experiment above produced exactly the mermaid-like outer loop. Separately, make the builder bow either check the full curve with bow_blocked() on the flat path too, or be replaced by an orthogonal outer-corridor polyline built from lay_ext (exit side vertex → ext±clear lane → enter target side), so the router never has to rescue it. The dagre-style alternative, a layout-level dummy chain for back edges ordered to the layer extremes, is L. After the change, run the tests/quality.rs gates and update the goldens.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Routes D->A out of the diamond's upper-right facet, right to x=980 outside Worker 5, up to y=77, and into Dispatcher's rightmost bottom port at x=615. No crossings.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The router replaces a node-clipping bow with an interior orthogonal path at the 12.5px minimum clearance. It goes up the gap between Worker 2 and Worker 3, crosses two fan-in edges, and enters Dispatcher's bottom in the middle of the fan-out.

verified.title: Two gap cuts 14px apart with opposite over/under make strokes look broken
verified.reasoning: Mask x6 cuts B2->C (black disc at 286.8,195.7, r=4.47). Mask x12 cuts D->A (disc at 286.8,209.4). The gaps are 13.7px apart and the over/under order flips between them. The 4x zoom (fanrev/z_mid.png) shows a gap in B2->C and a separate gap in the vertical loop line just below it, which reads as fragmentation. Both crossings exist only because of the loop-back route, so fixing that issue removes this one in this diagram. The casing rule is still a general defect.
verified.root_cause: /home/user/flowmaid/src/casing.rs:843-851 greedy_cost() adds (k-1)² per chain plus n² per line. Putting both gaps on D->A costs 1+4=5; splitting them costs 1+1=2. The greedy pick at casing.rs:517-533 compares grow() first, so the second crossing goes to the other line. The tie-break that sends the back edge under (casing.rs:525-526) only comes after the cost terms. Two gaps can never be a dash (DASH_RUN=3, quality.rs:74), so the split buys nothing visually.
verified.fix_sketch: In Assign::greedy, cluster crossings that sit on one shared line within about 3 gap widths (≈25px) and give the whole cluster the same under-line. Alternatively, move the ctx.back tie-break ahead of grow()/chain_with() whenever the move cannot create a dash chain (fewer than DASH_RUN gaps within GAP_PERIOD). Keep balance() from undoing it for back edges; it already skips back→forward moves.
verified.what_mermaid_does: There are no crossings, so no gaps are cut.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The under-edge is chosen per crossing to keep gap counts balanced, so two adjacent crossings on the same vertical line cut different strokes.

verified.title: Forward edges are smooth Beziers but the loop-back is an orthogonal polyline
verified.reasoning: All 12 forward edges are a single C segment. 'D -> A: no' is a chain of straight runs and small C corners. The waypoints after the nudge stage are corner-offset points 8.4px (first corner, limited by the 17px stub) and 14px apart. spline_d draws them as a uniform B-spline, which shrinks the visible radius to roughly 4–7px. Mermaid 12.2.0 uses orthogonal segments with 7.07px Q corners on every edge; B3->C and D->E are plain straight lines.
verified.root_cause: Two geometry generators are mixed. The builder draws free cubics: /home/user/flowmaid/src/scene.rs:3326-3343 (edge_points, down branch: [p0,(p0.0,p0.1+dl),(p3.0,p3.1-dl),p3]). Rerouted edges get orthogonal corners from router.rs:2570-2591 smooth(), with r = min(CORNER_R=14 / CORNER_MAX=36 (router.rs:236/240), half the shorter leg). The CORNER_MAX widening at router.rs:3846 is kept only if it scores no worse. These are painted by the basis spline in scene.rs:3738-3768 spline_d(), which never reaches the corner points, so short legs (the 17px diamond stub and the 12.5px jog) give tight corners. The router.rs:240 doc calls this an intended 'soft-orthogonal style next to the builder's free curves'.
verified.fix_sketch: Pick one family. For mermaid-12 parity (L): draw every flowchart edge as an orthogonal polyline with rounded corners, routing forward edges through their layer/channel points. The existing EdgeCurve::Rounded painter (scene.rs:376-392, ROUNDED_CURVE_RADIUS=5, raise to about 7–8) can be the default renderer. Cheaper (M): keep the cubics, give rerouted paths larger corners by enforcing a minimum leg of about 2×CORNER_R on stubs and jogs, and paint routed corners with exact quarter-curve cubics instead of the shrinking basis spline, so they read as the same soft family.
verified.what_mermaid_does: One style for all edges: orthogonal segments with about 7px quadratic rounded corners.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Builder edges are cubic S-curves. Router-rescued edges are orthogonal staircases with 4–7px basis-rounded corners.

verified.root_cause: /home/user/flowmaid/src/ports.rs:256-290 place(), the isotonic least-squares fit, moves every end of a group equally, so a straight edge's end is pushed off its line. The partner end on a lone side is never co-moved (ports.rs:460 skips lone ends). /home/user/flowmaid/src/edgepass.rs:309-321 runs ports::assign BEFORE router::repair. respace (spill_over=false) only re-places groups that became too close, so the spread computed for the pre-route ends survives after the router moves D->A.

If an edge's two ends sit on facing sides with |Δx| < PORT_SPACING and one of those sides holds a single end, move that end to the other's x within its flat range. Alternatively, weight aligned edges heavier in place() (weighted PAV) so the bent or back-edge end moves instead. (2) After router::repair, re-run a full assign (not respace) for every group whose membership or headings changed, so ends the router moved away leave no stale offsets.

name: long-labels
diagram_type: flowchart TD (5 nodes: rect, diamond, rounded, rect, circle; 2 labelled branch edges)
overall_verdict: Every element is drawn and nothing is broken. The output still looks worse than mermaid, and nearly all of that comes from one missing feature: flowmaid never wraps long labels. Because of that, node A becomes a 442x38 banner, the decision becomes a 616x65 sliver that barely reads as a diamond, and the canvas comes out nearly twice as wide as mermaid's (672 vs 358). The branch edges are also squeezed into the same 60px gap as unlabelled edges, so each one shows up as two small hooks poking out of its label chip, and the arrows land about 44px off-centre on their targets. Mermaid is less refined in places (grey label boxes, a tall diamond, awkward line breaks), but its composition reads cleanly and flowmaid's does not.
flowmaid_better: Vertically compact: 429px tall vs mermaid's 672px. Mermaid's 4-line wrapped diamond alone is 234x234 and takes a third of its height.
No awkward line breaks. Mermaid's 120px wrap leaves an orphan 'rules?' on its own line and splits 'Issue the / certificate'. Every flowmaid label reads as one phrase.

Edge label chips look cleaner: a white fill, a thin #d5d9ec border, rx=4 and 7px side padding. Mermaid uses a flat rgba(204,204,204,0.5) grey rectangle exactly as wide as the text ('incomplete' box 67.7px = text width), so the text touches the box edges.

Arrow tips touch the target border exactly (path ends at node top y=250.6, the tip overshoots about 0.6px into the stroke). Mermaid's pointEnd-margin markers stop about 4px short of the node (A->B path ends at y=156, diamond top at y=160), which leaves a visible gap.
Shape-based fills (amber decision, purple circle, teal rounded box) make the node types easy to tell apart at a glance. Mermaid's neo look is all black-on-white.
The lighter slate strokes (1.6 to 1.7px, #44507a) look more modern than mermaid's 2px pure-black lines.

verified.title: Plain node labels are never wrapped, which gives banner-shaped nodes and a canvas about twice as wide
verified.reasoning:
Checked against the SVGs. Flowmaid's A rect is 441.7x38, D is 245.8x38 and the canvas is 672 wide. Mermaid's A is 152.3x108, D 152x66, C 150x72, and its viewBox is 358 wide. The mermaid.svg div style reads 'display: table; white-space: break-spaces; max-width: 120px; width: 120px', and the mermaid 12.2.0 bundle sets `wrappingWidth": 120` by default. Flowmaid splits only on explicit newlines. To test this I re-rendered the same source with
inserted at mermaid's break points (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/rev_ll/wrapped.mmd). The canvas dropped to 345x583, close to mermaid's 358x672, and the diamond became 219.6x151.3. So wrapping alone fixes most of the visual gap, including the sliver diamond. One side finding: mermaid 12.2 renders labels at 14px (each line's foreignObject is 21px tall = 1.5 x 14px). Flowmaid's markdown wrap still converts with a 16px assumption (markdown.rs:24-31, 200*14/16 = 175px), so a new plain-label wrap should use 120px directly, not that 14/16 scaling.
verified.root_cause:
layout.rs:389 `let tw = node.label.split('\n').map(&measure).fold(0.0, f64::max)` sizes a node from its explicit lines only. parser.rs:217 normalize_breaks turns
into \n, and clean_label never inserts breaks. The only greedy wrap is markdown.rs:464 wrap_line (MD_WRAP_WIDTH, markdown.rs:31), which runs only for "`...`" strings and metadata labels.
verified.fix_sketch: After parsing a flowchart, for every node label that was not markdown-lowered, apply the greedy word wrap at NODE_WRAP_WIDTH = 120.0 flowmaid px. Mermaid 12.2 is 14px, so no 14/16 scaling. Measure with layout::text_width and keep explicit \n as hard breaks. Do not split an over-long word (mermaid keeps it whole). Factor markdown::wrap_line into a shared helper that takes a width. Apply it to every node shape, diamonds included, and leave edge labels alone; mermaid wraps those at 200, which can be a follow-up. Optionally read `flowchart.wrappingWidth` from an init directive or front-matter. <title> tooltips already join lines with spaces. Check the tests/quality.rs gates and any unit tests that assert byte-exact SVG for long-label fixtures. A later step (L) would wrap inside intrinsic_size_with using the injected measurer, so embedders with real fonts break at the right words.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Wraps plain HTML labels at a 120px max-width at 14px (mermaid 12.2 default wrappingWidth = 120). A comes out 152x108 over 4 lines, D 152x66 and C 150x72. The canvas is 358 wide.
verified.what_flowmaid_does:
Breaks only on explicit
/\n. A is one 441.7x38 line, D is 245.8x38 and the canvas is 672 wide.

verified.title: The decision diamond is a flat 9.5:1 sliver that alone sets the canvas width
verified.reasoning: The polygon in the SVG is '336,126 644,158.3 336,190.6 28,158.3': 616 wide by 64.6 tall, with faces sloping atan(32.3/308) = 6 degrees. It runs 87px past A on each side and 106.5px past C on the left. In the PNG it reads as a lens or banner. Mermaid's is a 234x234 square rhombus. Most of this follows from no-auto-wrap. With manual wrapping, flowmaid's own formula gives a reasonable 219.6x151.3 (1.45:1) diamond that holds the 4-line text. The height formula is still independent of width, so a long label that cannot wrap (one long word or code identifier, or a node after a wrap fix that still has a wide line) would still produce a sliver.
verified.root_cause: layout.rs:406 `Shape::Diamond => (((tw + 24.0) * 1.6).max(80.0), base_h * 1.7)`. Width grows linearly with text width, but height is BASE_H(38)*1.7 = 64.6 for any one-line label, whatever the width.
verified.fix_sketch: The main fix is no-auto-wrap. Separately, cap the aspect ratio: compute W as now, then H = max(base_h*1.7, W / 1.6), so the text still fits since a taller rhombus only gains room. Or follow mermaid's question shape, a square s = (tw + 2*pad) + (th + 2*pad). Check that ports.rs's Diamond profile (PORT_ROUND_SPAN) and the border() intersection still behave; both read bsize/lsize, so no code change is expected there.
verified.what_mermaid_does: A square rhombus (234x234) around the 4-line wrapped label.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: A 616x64.6 polygon around a one-line 361px label. It reads as a flat lens or banner and spans almost the full canvas.

verified.title: Labelled edges get the same 60px rank gap as unlabelled ones, so the arrowhead sits right under the label chip
verified.reasoning: Diamond bottom 190.6, chips at y 208.9..228.9, C/D tops at 250.6. That is 21.7px of straight drop above and below each chip, about 24.9px of curve on each side, and only about 14px of line between the chip and the 10.7px arrowhead. The A->B and C->E gaps are also exactly 60. Mermaid, measured vertex to top, gives 394->495 = 101px for the labelled rank against 40px for unlabelled A->B (2.5x), with about 25px of clear line between the label (y 434..455) and the arrowhead base. The first pass's '133px' measures from the exit point, but its conclusion holds. Experiment on a scratch copy: requiring 30px of run on each side of the chip (gap 80) made the drawing visibly closer to mermaid (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/rev_ll/ac.png and acw.png). This is a structural difference from dagre. Dagre gives labelled edges minlen 2, so the label becomes a dummy node in its own rank. Flowmaid sizes a label dummy only for long edges and gives adjacent-layer labelled edges none.
verified.root_cause: layout.rs:57 `GAP_L = 60.0` is used for every layer gap. layout.rs:1895-1911 grows the gap only when `at - ends < ext` (label extent 20px), and then only to ext + 2*LABEL_CLEAR (6px, layout.rs:163). layout.rs:1396-1408 reserves a label-sized middle dummy only for long edges (chain non-empty). rank() at layout.rs:989 has no minlen, so a labelled adjacent edge never gets its own label rank.
verified.fix_sketch: Cheap fix (validated): in the short_labels loop, for TD/BT require `at - ends >= ext + 2.0*LABEL_RUN` with LABEL_RUN = ARROW_MARKER_PX + ~18 (about 30), and set cursor to `ends + ext + 2*LABEL_RUN - lh/2`. Keep the current rule for LR/RL, where ext is the label width. Re-tune the tests/quality.rs ceilings. Dagre-faithful alternative (L): add minlen=2 for labelled edges in rank() (a weighted step in the longest-path loop) so every labelled edge gets a middle dummy sized by the existing layout.rs:1396 code. Its label then rides a slot that BK aligns with the target, as in mermaid. This also fixes hooked-label-stubs and off-centre-arrivals.
verified.what_mermaid_does: The labelled rank is about 101px (vertex to child top) against 40px unlabelled. The label sits on a straight run with about 25px of clear line before the arrowhead.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Every gap is 60px. The 20px chip leaves about 21.7px above and below, and the arrowhead base is about 14px under the chip.

verified.title: Labels cover the diagonal middle of a tight S-curve, so each edge shows as two disconnected hooks
verified.reasoning: I recomputed the bezier 'M 303.6 187.2 C 303.6 218.9, 254.9 218.9, 254.9 250.6' numerically. It crosses the chip's top (y 208.9) at x = 293.1 and its bottom (y 228.9) at x = 265.4. That is 13.8px either side of the chip centre 279.2; the first pass said about 16px. The chip covers t = 0.30..0.70, the steepest stretch of the S. The visible parts are about 25px each: a curl out of the diamond and a curl into the arrowhead. The 4x zoom (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/rev_ll/fm_zoom.png) shows the hooks clearly. With a larger gap the curve reads as more continuous (acw.png), but the label still sits on the diagonal. Mermaid puts it on the final vertical leg of an orthogonal route with rounded corners.
verified.root_cause: scene.rs:3327-3344 builds the adjacent-layer edge as one cubic [p0, (p0.x, p0.y+dl), (p3.x, p3.y-dl), p3] with dl = half the drop. Its x-profile is a smoothstep, steepest at t = 0.5. The label goes to t = 0.5: cubic_mid at scene.rs:3726, or labels.rs:84 LABEL_PREFER = 0.5. Clean labels keep that slot, and LABEL_HUB_PREFER (labels.rs:88, 1520-1533) applies only to labels the placer frees. The 48.7px lateral offset comes from the diamond source anchoring toward the target's centre (scene.rs:3286, border()) while the rect target anchor is biased only 35% back toward the source (scene.rs:3293). The short drop comes from the 60px gap (see labels-crammed-in-gap).
verified.fix_sketch: For labelled adjacent-layer edges in TD/BT, after growing the gap: route as a two-piece path. Put the S-bend in the upper part, from p0 to (p3.x, label_top - LABEL_CLEAR), then a straight vertical run through the label to p3, and place the label centre on that straight run. SceneEdge already supports multi-segment curves (curve_geometry/Seg in scene.rs:361). Ports and labels passes take segment lists, so the shape needs to be emitted from edge_points/scene_from_layout plus the label point. Alternatively, take the minlen-2 label-dummy approach from labels-crammed-in-gap; the edge then routes through a dummy aligned with the target via spline_d, and the label rides it.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Orthogonal route with a horizontal jog above the label. The label sits on the vertical leg into the target, so the line enters it top-centre and leaves bottom-centre.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Single S-bezier with the chip over its diagonal middle. The line enters the chip 13.8px right of centre and leaves 13.8px left, and only two curved stubs show.

verified.reasoning: B->C ends at x = 254.9 on C (centre 211.2) and B->D at 417.1 on D (centre 460.8). C->E leaves C at 211.2, so the line into C and the line out of it are 43.7px apart. verified.root_cause: scene.rs:3293 in anchor(): `let bias = ((other.0 - p.b) * 0.35 + off).clamp(-flat, flat);`. Every rect-like end, the target included, is pulled 35% of the centre-to-centre offset toward the other node. The ports pass (ports.rs) re-spreads only ends that crowd a side, so a lone arrival keeps the bias.
verified.fix_sketch: Drop the bias (use only `off`) for an end that is alone on its node side; the ports pass already spreads sides holding several ends (PORT_SPACING 14). At minimum, zero it for a single incoming edge on a node that also has an outgoing edge on the opposite side, which keeps the spine straight. Ship it together with the labels-crammed-in-gap gap growth so the S does not get steeper. Then check the quality gates (crossings and node hits) in tests/quality.rs.

verified.what_flowmaid_does: Arrivals at 254.9 and 417.1 against centres 211.2 and 460.8, both pulled 43.7px toward the diamond. C->E leaves from C's centre, which leaves a 43.7px jog through C.

verified.title: Arrowheads are about 25% narrower and lighter than mermaid's
verified.reasoning: Flowmaid's #arrow uses viewBox 10x10, markerWidth/Height 7 in strokeWidth units at a stroke of 1.7 (11.9px box, scale 1.19), and path 'M 0 1 L 9 5 L 0 9'. That gives 10.7px long by 9.5px wide. Mermaid's pointEnd-margin uses userSpaceOnUse with viewBox 11.5x14 and markerWidth 10.5 / markerHeight 14 (uniform scale 0.913), path 11.5x14, giving 10.5 x 12.8px. Flowmaid's is 26% narrower, as claimed. In the side-by-side, flowmaid's heads look small but are clearly visible, so this is cosmetic.

overall_verdict: Up close, flowmaid's parts look better than mermaid's. Its label chips are neater, its nodes are softly filled, each edge gets its own attachment point, and long labels stay on one line. In LR that axis is vertical, so the label's height (20px) should be used, not its 337px width. The same mistake appears in src/layout.rs:2138-2142 (drawn_breadth, which estimates the drawn breadth for centring) and in src/scene.rs:730 (bow_blocked, clustered pipeline). name: fanout-frames
diagram_type: flowchart LR: one source fanning out to 6 subgraphs (each `direction TB`, no internal edges) plus one plain node
overall_verdict:
Node by node, flowmaid looks cleaner than mermaid. It keeps the source's
breaks instead of squeezing labels into tall narrow boxes, its shapes are well proportioned, and the semantic fills make stadiums and cylinders easy to spot. The ugliness is in how the diagram is put together and how the edges are drawn. The narrowing pass pushes g3 into a second column, so its edge takes a long detour squeezed between frames. The seven fan-out edges mix steep S-curves with rounded right-angle elbows, two crossings that could be avoided are drawn with gap masks that look like broken lines, and arrows hit a ragged column of faint frames at arbitrary heights. Mermaid's left-aligned comb of right-angle edges is taller, but it reads much more orderly and has no crossings.
flowmaid_better:
Keeps the author's
breaks and does not re-wrap: the cylinder n1 is 3 lines and 228px wide in flowmaid, while mermaid makes it a narrow 8-line tower. 'elit elit ipsum magna...' is 3 lines vs 6 in mermaid. Labels are much easier to read.
Smaller overall canvas: 838x1661 vs mermaid's 648x2271 viewBox, about 27% less height, with no extreme vertical strip.
Semantic shape fills (stadiums green #e5f5ea/#33a35c, cylinders blue #e7eef7/#4d8fbf, rects #eef1fb/#5b6dc0) show shape types at a glance. Mermaid draws everything white with black outlines.

No empty grid cells inside frames: mermaid's g1 grid leaves the cylinder alone in its row with a blank cell beside it, and the g3 grid is uneven. Flowmaid's single centered column inside each frame looks tidy.
The dashed `-.->` edge (dasharray 5 4) stands out more than mermaid's 2px dotted line.
Flat, crisp rendering with no drop shadows. Cluster titles are left-aligned 12px bold on a backing pill, so edges never cut through them.
Softer edge color (#44507a, 1.7px) is easier on the eye than mermaid's black 2px lines.

verified.title: Subgraph g3 is pushed into a second column although it is the same rank as its siblings
verified.reasoning: In flowmaid.svg the g3 rect is at x=548.7 while g1/g2/g4/g5/g6 sit at x=261-286. Mermaid puts all six frames at x=244. Two corrections to the first pass. (1) The n0->g3 path is about 725px long, not 900 (mermaid's is 433). (2) Narrowing did not save space. I rebuilt a scratch copy with RIBBON_ENTRY=1e9 (scratchpad/fmx_fanframes/nonarrow.svg) and got a single column at 550x2311 = 1.27M px². The narrowed drawing is 838x1661 = 1.39M px², 9% MORE area, plus two empty regions and a detour edge. The ribbon test fired only barely, at a breadth/depth ratio of about 4.1-4.2 against a threshold of 4.0.
verified.root_cause: src/layout.rs:505 runs narrow() when total_b > RIBBON_ENTRY(4.0, line 85) * total_l. A hub feeding a column of tall frames is only 2 layers deep, so it always looks like a ribbon. narrow() step 1, sibling stacking (layout.rs:600-650), takes the pairs from stack_candidates (layout.rs:879-985), ranked by gain = min(breadth of the two boxes), so g1/g3 rank first and g3 gets a rank-only group placing it one rank after g1. The acceptance closure `better` (layout.rs:593) checks only three things: breadth drops by at least 3%, skeleton crossings stay within crossing_budget(0)=0, and node hits. It never checks canvas area, total edge length, or the crossings the router will actually draw. The layout reported 0 crossings for this candidate; the final SVG has 2 crossing masks.
verified.fix_sketch: In `better`, also require total_b*total_l not to grow by more than about 2%, and charge each stacked box for the extra length of its incoming edges, which now span 2 ranks. Better still, for a fan of sibling frames that share one rank, offer a wrap candidate before stacking: split the column into 2 columns at the SAME rank, with no new rank and no detour. Optionally raise RIBBON_ENTRY when the drawing has 2 or fewer layers.

verified.what_flowmaid_does: Moves g3 one rank to the right of g1 (x=548.7). This adds area instead of saving it and forces a long detour edge.

verified.title: The n0->g3 detour hugs frame borders and ends with the arrowhead sitting in the bend

The horizontal at y=602.5 runs 12.5px under g1 (bottom 590) and 7.5px over g2 (top 610), so it reads as a double top border on g2. The vertical at x=534.2 is 14.5px from g3. The arrowhead sits right after the corner. One correction: the straight run after the corner is about 12px (536.6 to 548.7), not 8, which leaves about 2px of shaft before the 10.1px head base. Instrumenting the router showed this is not just a narrowing effect. Weighted A* returned a path costing 1264 when a cheaper one (1250) existed. With H_WEIGHT=1.0 (scratchpad/fmx_fanframes/expH.svg) the edge goes through the 40px gap between g2 and g4, rises at x=524 into g3, and crosses nothing.

It stops at the first path within 1.5x of optimal, which here is the upward run through the 20px g1/g2 gap (FRAME_GAP 8 + 2x pad). (b) Before routing, the layout had already placed the g3 stand-in's layer-1 dummy at (388.9, 932), level with n0 and between g2 and g4. The stand-in targets n9 (scene.rs:1034, the first declared entry member), so the built path's last segment, (388.9,932) to (548.7,664), cuts diagonally through g2 (debug score node:2 frame:1) and must be repaired. (c) Nothing makes the final leg at least as long as the arrowhead plus the corner radius: the last vertical leg lands on the lattice track FRAME_SEP (14) off the target frame, and smooth() (router.rs:2570) clamps the radius to half of that leg.

Add a lattice track at border - (ARROW_MARKER_PX + CORNER_R + 4) beside target ends, or have nudge() pull the last leg back when the channel allows, so the final leg is at least 24px. Longer term, the stand-in dummy should be ordered next to its target member's breadth.
