verified.title: The seven fan-out edges mix steep cubic S-curves with rounded right-angle elbows
verified.reasoning: n0->g1, g2, g4 and g5 are each a single C segment with control points at the mid-gap x (for example 238.0/238.0 for g1: a 351px rise over a 46px run). n0->g3, g6 and n21 are orthogonal with 6px corners. A debug dump of each finish() stage showed that all 7 edges start as cubics, and only the 3 that the router flagged are redrawn orthogonally: g3 for node and frame hits, n21 for node:1 and frame:1 (its S-curve cut through g6), and g6 for an overlap with the g5 curve.
verified.root_cause: src/scene.rs:1460-1536, sub_edge_ported(): a box-targeted edge with no channel becomes one cubic, with `let dl = (p3.1 - p0.1) * 0.5` (scene.rs:1533), i.e. controls at half the 46px flow gap whatever the breadth offset (up to 351px). Then router::repair (router.rs:4166 onward) reroutes only the 'bad' edges and leaves clean curves exactly as built, by design (module docs, router.rs lines 7-8). So each edge's style depends on whether it happened to collide, not on the fan it belongs to.
verified.fix_sketch: Bundle the fan. When 3 or more edges leave the same side of a node toward one layer, draw them all as orthogonal elbows with nested channels: sort the up-going and down-going halves by |Δbreadth| and give the farthest-turning edges the channels nearest the source. That gives a mermaid-style comb with no crossings by construction, and the router treats these edges as accepted. A cheaper interim fix: if the router reroutes any edge of a fan, redraw its siblings orthogonally too. Widening GAP_L for fans (m*EDGE_SEP) would give the comb room.

verified.title: Two crossings that could be avoided, drawn with gap masks that look like broken lines
verified.reasoning: There are two masks: one at (253.5, 893.5) on n0->g2 and one at (220.1, 1357) on n0->g6. Both breaks are clearly visible in the zooms (zff/n0left.png, zff/x6.png). Mermaid has 0 crossings. Experiments: with H_WEIGHT=1.0 the g2/g3 crossing disappears, because g3 takes the g2/g4 gap. The n21/g6 crossing remains (mask at 121.5, 1355), because the order of n0's bottom-side ports puts g6 on the outer-left (107.5) and n21, the edge that travels farther, on the inner side (121.5).
verified.root_cause: x2: a consequence of the weighted-A* detour (router.rs:227), which puts g3's vertical at x=253.5 right across g2's short S-curve. x6: router::repair routes edges in the order 'hard before soft, short before long' (router.rs ~4272). n21 (hard) is routed first and takes the bottom midpoint. g6 then gets a neighbouring slot from free_slot/respace, and nothing enforces L-shape nesting. The static reorder pass, ports::reorder via place_ports, keys each end by heading_on (ports.rs:692) toward the first off-axis waypoint (end_and_steer, ports.rs:292). For two L-paths turning the same way this does not model 'whoever turns later goes outside', and n21's spurious jog skews its key further.
verified.fix_sketch: Comb routing for fans (see the mixed-style finding) removes both crossings by construction. Short of that: (1) set H_WEIGHT=1.0 for static scenes; (2) for ends on the same side whose paths turn the same way, order them by turn distance, so the later turn sits on the outer slot. Apply it in ports::reorder, or as a swap test inside repair after both edges are routed.
verified.what_mermaid_does: No crossings. The channels nest at x=184/204/224.

verified.title: Two edges leave n0's bottom while five leave its right side, and n0->n21 takes an unneeded S-jog
verified.reasoning: g6 and n21 start at (107.5 / 121.5, 959.5) on n0's bottom face. Instrumenting the A* showed that n21's 3-bend path costs 972 while the 1-bend L (straight down at x=121.5, then right at y=1614) costs 924, and every lattice step on that L was free (step()=Some(0.0)). The greedy heuristic simply stopped early. With H_WEIGHT=1.0, n21 became the single L. Forcing SIDE_SWITCH_COST=1e5 kept every exit on the right face, but n21 then ran down a lane 5-8px from the frames (expA.svg). So side choice alone does not fix it; the free curves crowding the right-side channel do.

overall_verdict: flowmaid draws every element and is much more compact than mermaid: about 43% of the canvas area and 44% of the total edge length. Up close, though, it looks worse. Mermaid's output is huge and full of long parallel edge bundles, but it reads as one consistent system: every edge is orthogonal, and each cluster has its own color. flowmaid mixes three edge styles (orthogonal, long flat S-curves and freeform splines), knots the edges under the hub node, punches gaps into crossing lines, lets some edges overlap and crowds arrowheads together. Its clusters all share one pale color, sit inside each other as outlines 14 units apart, and have large empty middles. Most of the "ugly" feeling comes from edge routing that is inconsistent and unfinished, plus flat cluster styling. Nothing is missing or semantically wrong.
flowmaid_better: Far more compact: viewBox 4249x1823 (7.7M units²) vs mermaid 4130x4378 (18.1M). Total edge length is 58.7k vs 134.8k units, and the longest edge is 3316 (n45→g8) vs 7717 (mermaid's n43→n16). Mermaid draws large bundles of parallel lines running thousands of units.

Nodes keep the author's

verified.title: Three edge styles mixed: orthogonal routes, long flat S-curves, freeform splines
verified.reasoning: I re-parsed all 47 paths. 20 are a single cubic. Many of them are extremely flat: n31→n38 is dx 2593 / dy 146, n22→n40 is 2857/144, n25→n42 is 2349/120, n16→n23 is 1722/118 and n33→n16 is 999/60. 19 are orthogonal with rounded corners (flowmaid's own quality yardstick also reports ortho_edges=19). 5 are freeform basis splines: n16→n37, n36→n16, n5→n44, n41→n42 and n46→n17. In mermaid 12.2.0 every one of the 47 paths uses only axis-aligned L/Q segments plus 60 hop arcs.
verified.root_cause:
There are three separate sources, and nothing makes them one style.
(1) scene.rs:853-858: an edge between adjacent layers gets no waypoints, and edge_points (scene.rs:3344) returns `[p0,(p0.0,p0.1+dl),(p3.0,p3.1-dl),p3]`. That is a single vertical-tangent cubic however large dx is, which produces the flat S-curves.
(2) An edge spanning several layers gets the virtual-node chain as waypoints and is drawn as a curveBasis spline (basis_sample, scene.rs:518), which produces the freeform curves.
(3) router::repair 'leaves every good edge exactly as the builder drew it' (router.rs:7-8, acceptance at 4210-4262). It only turns broken edges into orthogonal corner paths (smooth, router.rs:2570).
It gets worse because the router's Score is lexicographic (node, frame, chip, wiggle, overlap…; router.rs:443-472) and `better` (router.rs:4515) refuses frame-for-overlap trades. I added debug prints in a scratch copy: for n31→n38, n25→n42, n22→n40 and n16→n23 every orthogonal candidate kept the same unavoidable frame count with more overlap (e.g. 675→1831), so the flat cubic stayed. A 50× larger work budget changed nothing, so the router is not running out of budget.
verified.fix_sketch:
Pick one house style, orthogonal like mermaid, in Static mode:
(a) In scene_from_layout, give adjacent-layer edges with |dx|>~20 Z-waypoints [p0,(p0.x,ymid),(p3.x,ymid),p3]. Turn virtual-node chains into vertical runs through each dummy's x, joined by horizontal jogs at the rank-gap midline.
(b) Hand every edge to nudge() as an orthogonal path so spread() separates the shared gap channels.
(c) Grow GAP_L per rank gap with the number of horizontal legs crossing it (count × EDGE_SEP). A fixed 60 cannot hold about 15 legs.
(d) Let the router compare overlap/tight before frame when the frame count is the same for every candidate.
A cheaper interim step: Z-route any single cubic with |dx|/|dy| > 3.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Flat single cubics that run 600-2860 units across with a 60-150 unit drop. Orthogonal rounded routes only where the router repaired an edge. Basis splines for the remaining multi-rank edges.
verified.what_mermaid_does: All 47 edges are orthogonal with 5-7px rounded corners, and 60 crossings are marked with hop arcs.

verified.title: Edges knot together under the hub node n16
verified.reasoning:
Verified in the crop at 1880-2260 × 960-1260.
- n21→n16 bows left to x=1978.9, outside g4's left border at 1983, and arrives at about -40°.
- n16→n29 drops from 2033, jogs to 1997.5, then runs left at y=1157.4.
- n31→n16 makes a lateral hairpin at y≈1157: its vertices go x 2083→2057→2075.
- The 'elit' label box (2020.8-2053.3) has its own edge running inside its right edge at x≈2051.6, while the n16→n29 line sits 23 units to its left.
- n16's bottom ends sit at 2005, 2019, 2033, 2047, 2061, 2075, 2089 and 2110: seven ends 14 apart, packed into the left 113 units of the 161-unit side.
verified.root_cause:
There are four mechanisms.
(a) n21→n16 is an adjacent-layer back-edge, drawn with the general back-edge bow (scene.rs:3349-3370: apex 24px + label beyond the layer extents, `[p0,(bt,p0.1-40),(bt,p3.1+40),p3]`). Nothing lies between the two nodes, but the bow still swings outside g4. The router scored it clean and kept it.
(b) anchor() (scene.rs:3293) clamps `bias = 0.35*dx` to ±(w/2-12), so every left-heading edge anchors at n16's left end. The isotonic min-move fit in ports.rs (header lines 1-11, PORT_SPACING=14 at ports.rs:23) then packs the ends rightward from the inset instead of spreading them over the side.
(c) Rerouted edges leave those packed ports and step to lattice tracks placed at node bounds ± ROUTE_CLEAR. straighten folds only jogs ≤ PORT_JOG_MAX=20 (router.rs:2859), which produces the 35-unit jog on n16→n29.
(d) Wiggle scoring counts only backtracking along the flow axis (router.rs:855-867; quality.rs:1207-1225), so the sideways hairpin on n31→n16 costs nothing.
verified.fix_sketch:
1. For a back-edge between adjacent layers with a free vertical corridor, draw an orthogonal up-route from a dedicated port instead of the bow (S).
2. For a side with ≥3 ends, spread them over the usable span in heading order rather than doing a min-move fit from clamped anchors (M).
3. Add a cross-axis reversal term to Score.wiggle and to the quality metric: a sign change of lateral direction within ~40px counts as a wiggle (S).
4. The orthogonalisation in mixed-edge-geometry fixes the n16→n23 sweep.

The doc comment says this is meant for back-edges, but it applies to forward edges too. n16's bottom is already full, so the A* exits through the sides. ports::respace then spaces those ends at PORT_SPACING 14 (ports.rs:23), filling the 72-unit side (8 inset + 4×14). So the real problem is crowding at the hub; a constant change does not fix it.

1. Allow alternate sides only for back-edges and sideways edges in TB, or price forward side exits by flow deviation.
2. Give a hub a wider port span. Either let the edges fan out through a short shared trunk below the node, or widen the node's port band when degree × PORT_SPACING exceeds its width.
3. Make spread() label-aware: a labelled leg keeps LABEL_BOX_H/2 + EDGE_SEP from its neighbours.

verified.title: Different edges share or almost share the same path
verified.reasoning:
In the path data, n28→n42 and n29→n38 both run at y=1495.4 for x≈1410-1468, exactly on top of each other. A 2-unit proximity scan found:
- n15→n38 / n25→n42: ~196px within 3 units (x 2260-2451)
- n16→n23 (solid) / n22→n40 (dashed): ~90px (x 1404-1492)
- n11→n37 / n25→n42: ~70px
- n8→n42 / n28→n42: ~36px
flowmaid's own quality report for this file gives overlap_pairs=14, overlap_len=1734 and tight_pairs=17 / 3920px. In the PNG, n28's edge visibly merges into n29→n38's line and then splits, which reads like a junction.
verified.root_cause: router::repair accepts each clean edge against only the edges accepted so far, with channel edges first and then in index order (router.rs:4200, 4210-4262). n15→n38 and n11→n37 score clean and are accepted before the 'hard' n25→n42. When n25→n42 comes up, every candidate must still cross 3 foreign frames, and `better` (router.rs:4515-4545) rejects candidates with more overlap (debug: base 675, best 1831). Both edges keep their overlap, and the clean partner is never re-searched. The coincident y=1495.4 stretch comes from two rerouted edges that spread() (router.rs:3135) did not separate. Most likely the short n28→n42 leg is a port-leg jog inside the channel that FRAME_SEP squeezes against g6's bottom border; I did not confirm this.
verified.fix_sketch: After the first repair, run a second pass over every edge that is still in an overlap or tight pair, including the earlier-accepted clean partner, and allow either member to move. verified.title: The LR diagram no longer reads left to right: zones are stacked into a portrait block
verified.reasoning: Re-measured. Frame rects: app (373,96), data (494,1041) directly below app, jobs (1119,1591), ops (1110,60). Canvas is 1772x2017. Direction tally from node centres: right 33, down 22, up 14, left 6, exactly as claimed. `direction TB` has no effect: the output is byte-identical with those lines removed, and mermaid ignores it too for clusters with external edges. I simulated flowmaid's rank() in Python and it reproduces the drawn layers exactly: user0 gw1 lb2 {svc1,3,5,6}3 db4 svc2 5 cache6 svc4 7 queue8 {metrics,job1-3}9 {objects,alerts}10 logs11 dash12 ext13. So the app zone spans layers 3-7 and the data zone spans 4-10. Those spans overlap, so cluster contiguity forces the zones side by side on the breadth axis, which is vertical in LR. Experiment: a private copy with greedy FAS plus sifting in place of the DFS (built in scratchpad/rv75b/fm, output rv75b/fas.svg) gives canvas 1414x1372 instead of 1772x2017 and 47.6k px of edges instead of 65.4k. svc1..svc6 become one column. The data zone still splits into 2 layers with jobs between them, because job->db is now forward. So mermaid's look also needs cluster-aware ranking. (Housekeeping: I accidentally re-copied the pristine repo src into the shared scratchpad/fmcopy. git there shows it equals HEAD.)
verified.root_cause: src/layout.rs:1016-1047 (rank, step 1). Back edges are picked by an iterative DFS in node-declaration and edge order. DFS goes user->gw->lb->svc1->db and then follows db->svc2 and cache->svc4 as tree edges. It therefore marks the majority-direction edges svc2->db, svc4->db and svc4->cache as back edges, along with job1/2/3->db, alerts->gw, dash->user and job1->svc1: 9 reversals where 5 suffice. Then src/layout.rs:1049-1074, longest-path layering with no cluster compaction, spreads every zone over many layers: data 4-10, ops 9-12. Overlapping cluster spans cannot sit in sequence along the flow, so they stack on the breadth axis. narrow() (layout.rs:563) does not fire here, because total_b < 4*total_l.
verified.fix_sketch: (1) Replace the DFS FAS with a weighted Eades-Lin-Smyth greedy FAS (bucket version, O(m)), followed by a sifting or adjacent-swap local search that minimises the number of reversed edges, with ties broken by declaration index. Prototype result: the app column is restored in declaration order. (2) Make layering cluster-aware. Either run network simplex with dagre-style nesting edges, or run a post-pass that shrinks each subgraph's layer span, preferring to reverse a cross-cluster edge over stretching a cluster across 3+ layers (mermaid reverses job->db, which keeps data in one rank).
verified.what_mermaid_does: Zones edge, app, data, jobs, ops and ext run strictly left to right. 65 of 75 edges point right.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Data sits below app, jobs below data, ops top-right. Only 33 of 75 edges point right, on a portrait 1772x2017 canvas.

(c) router.rs:4218-4266 (repair trigger) re-routes an edge only on hard hits (node, frame or chip), overlap, near, or hug/tight. Crossings, shape, steep diagonals and style consistency are never triggers, so clean free curves survive next to orthogonal reroutes.

Either orthogonalise every builder channel edge (turn the dummy chain into an axis-aligned polyline that bends at the inter-layer midlines and feed it to the nudge), or add a soft class-1 trigger in repair() for free curves whose breadth span is more than about 3x their layer span, or whenever the scene already contains orthogonal reroutes. (3) Port crowding: LR nodes are BASE_H=38px tall (layout.rs:50), and ports.rs:23-37 (PORT_SPACING 14, PORT_INSET 8, falling to PORT_INSET_MIN 4 and PORT_MIN_SPACING 6) pack 4-5 ends onto a 38px side, pushing the outer ends to 4px from the corners. anchor() (scene.rs:3293) also biases builder ends toward the far node.

Grow LR node height to fit the side's degree, max(BASE_H, (n-1)*PORT_SPACING + 2*PORT_INSET), so ports keep at least 8px from corners.

name: class
diagram_type: classDiagram
overall_verdict: Next to mermaid, flowmaid's class diagram is smaller and fits on one screen (774x636 against 569x1412), but it reads worse. The hierarchy is upside down: superclasses, the interface and the composite all sit below their children. The note and the «interface» stereotype are missing. The 'charges' dependency swings out in a big arc and its arrowhead is half hidden under the PaymentMethod box. One edge crosses another, edges hook in at box corners, and the multiplicity labels sit on top of the lines. On the boxes, the white header text has low contrast and the grey compartment lines are so faint that empty compartments look like a rendering glitch. Mermaid is tall and has a lot of empty space, but its layout follows UML convention, it has no crossings and its orthogonal routing is consistent.
flowmaid_better: Much more compact: viewBox 774x636 (aspect about 1.2) against mermaid's 569x1412 (aspect 0.40). The whole model fits on one screen with no 430px-long edges like mermaid's 'owns' run down the right side.

The trailing '%% dependency at checkout' is stripped, so the label reads just 'charges'. Mermaid prints the comment text as a two-line label, 'charges %% dependency at checkout', which is clearly not what the author meant (the file header calls it a comment).
Edge labels sit on white rounded pills (rect rx=4, stroke #d5d9ec) that hide the line underneath, so labels never have a stroke running through them.
Solid coloured header bands make the class names stand out at a glance more than mermaid's pastel fills do (but see the contrast issue).
Hollow inheritance and realization triangles are 16x14 px, larger and easier to read than mermaid's small triangle markers.
Tiny output (8.9 KB SVG against 54 KB) with no embedded CSS or animation keyframes.

verified.title: UML hierarchy is upside down: parents, the interface and the composite rank below their children
verified.reasoning: Confirmed in the SVG and the probe dump. The parser turns `Person <|-- Customer` into Customer->Person, `Order *-- LineItem` into LineItem->Order, and `Customer o-- PaymentMethod` into PaymentMethod->Customer, so in TD layout every decorated class sits one rank lower. Mermaid 12.2 builds every class edge as `start: classRelation.id1, end: classRelation.id2` (classDiagram-v2 chunk, lines 1901-1902), so it ranks by left operand -> right operand. I tested this by rewriting the operators so flowmaid's from equals the left operand (scratchpad/cls_probe/swapped.mmd). flowmaid then produced mermaid's topology: Person > Customer > Order > LineItem/PaymentMethod > Product/CreditCard/PayPal, with zero crossings and no arc.
verified.root_cause: parser.rs:3302-3307 rewrites (from,to) so that the decorated end is always `to` (head_left swaps the operands). class.rs:134 `g.add_edge(r.from, r.to, ...)` then feeds that semantic direction straight into the layered layout. For <|--, *--, o-- and <|.. this reverses mermaid's source-order ranking. It also creates a cycle, PaymentMethod->Customer->Order->PaymentMethod, that mermaid's graph does not have.
verified.fix_sketch: Add `head_at_from: bool` (or keep `left`/`right` indices) to model::ClassRel and set it from head_left in parse_class_relation. In class::build, add the layout edge in source order: (left, right) = if head_left {(to, from)} else {(from, to)}. In to_svg, draw the glyph at q[0]/q[1] instead of q[3]/q[2] when the decorated end is the edge start, and swap the card ends to match. name: state
diagram_type: stateDiagram-v2 (composite state with inner direction LR, choice, fork/join, note, start/end, transition labels)
overall_verdict: At the level of individual elements, flowmaid looks cleaner than mermaid here: the edge labels are tidier, the colours are calmer, there are no shadow or double-border artifacts, and it draws <<choice>> and <<fork>> the way the source asks, which mermaid 12.2 does not. The diagram as a whole looks worse for two reasons. First, flowmaid silently drops the note ("shown to the user"), so information is lost. Second, it ignores `direction LR` inside the Validating composite. That turns a 459x109 row into a 126x368 column, and the canvas becomes a skinny 403x1133 strip (aspect 0.36, against mermaid's 649x886 at 0.73). The edges add more problems: the retry arc's arrowheads graze the box borders, the fork/join branches wiggle in S-curves, the "submit" edge has a pointless kink that runs under its own label, the labels under an oversized empty diamond are crammed together, and node widths are uneven.
flowmaid_better: Correct semantics for `state decide <<choice>>` and `state forked <<fork>>`. mermaid 12.2.0 keeps these as ordinary states because they are used in a transition before they are declared: its SVG has `statediagram-state` boxes labelled 'decide' and 'forked', 136x37 each. Flowmaid draws a diamond and a fork bar as the source intends. Do not copy mermaid here for the sake of parity.

Edge labels are white rounded pills (rx 4, stroke #d5d9ec) that sit cleanly on or beside the stroke. In mermaid the labels are grey rectangles that the line runs into: 'ok' is squeezed between Syntax and Semantics with the stroke touching both sides, and 'submit', 'retry', 'valid' and 'invalid' are grey blocks cut into the lines.

Clean arrow endings. Mermaid's orthogonal routes put a rounded corner right before the arrowhead, which leaves curled hook-shaped tips at Idle (retry, around png 608,175) and Rejected (invalid, around png 795,725). Flowmaid's tips are straight.
Single clean composite border. Mermaid draws an outer rect (ending at y=313) and an inner rect (ending at y=309), which shows as a doubled pink line along the bottom of Validating.
The 'invalid' transition is a short direct curve. Mermaid routes it through a three-elbow detour: decide, then right, down, right and down into Rejected.
The colour scheme works: teal states, an amber choice and slate edges with good text contrast (#232840 on #e4f5f4). Flowmaid also avoids mermaid's drop shadows and its loud magenta cluster.
Total area is smaller (403x1133 = 457k units² against mermaid's 649x886 = 575k), and no edge crosses another.

verified.title: `direction LR` inside a composite (and inside any flowchart subgraph) has no effect on layout
verified.reasoning: I deleted the `direction LR` line and re-rendered. The output is byte-identical. The cluster rect is 126.1x368 and every inner node sits at x=218.3. Mermaid gives a 459x109 row. I also checked a plain flowchart (`flowchart TB; X-->s; subgraph s direction LR; A-->B-->C end; s-->Y`): A, B and C still stack vertically at x=42, so this is a general engine limitation and not specific to state diagrams.
verified.root_cause: scene.rs:1018 scene_clustered runs one global Sugiyama pass over every real node in g.direction (layout_clustered_ranked, line ~1047). There is no recursive per-cluster layout. Subgraph.direction (set at parser.rs:4871-4876) is read in only two places: layout.rs:1199-1209 (stagger_proposals, where it only pins members against staggering) and scene.rs:1621 (grid_pairs, where it only skips grid packing). Neither changes the axis the members are laid out on.
verified.fix_sketch: Use a dagre/mermaid-style compound layout for subgraphs whose direction differs from the parent's and whose members have no node-to-node edges crossing the border. In state diagrams composite edges are sub_edges, so this is the common case; when edges do cross, fall back to the current behaviour, as mermaid does. Steps: (1) build a child Graph from the members, their internal edges and nested subgraphs, with direction = sub.direction, and run scene_sized on it; (2) in the parent, collapse the members into one proxy node sized to the child bbox + 2*FRAME_PAD + header; (3) lay out the parent and route sub_edges to the proxy; (4) translate the child scene into the proxy box, splice nodes back into index-parallel order, emit the frame, then run edgepass::finish. The extra work is in keeping the Scene index-parallel and in route_partial/drag consistency.

verified.what_flowmaid_does: Stacks the inner chain vertically: a 126x368 cluster in a 403x1133 canvas (aspect 0.36).

verified.title: Retry back-edge is a single wide cubic with near-horizontal end tangents, and both of its ports sit on the wrong side
verified.reasoning: The path is `M171.1 724.6 C30.3 684.6, 28.0 180.0, 196.7 140.0`. Its end tangent (P3-P2) is 13.3 degrees above horizontal and its start tangent is about 16 degrees. The marker is 11.9 units long (7 x stroke 1.7). At 13 degrees, one back corner of the arrowhead lands at about y=138.1, which is 1.9 units inside Idle's box. Nodes are painted after edges, so that corner is covered and the head looks clipped against the border. The zoomed crop agrees. One detail is overstated: the curve does not hug Rejected's top for about 40 units. Sampling puts it within 10 units of the top only from x=171 to about 151 (t<0.05), and 25 units above by x=133. The real problem at Rejected is that the arc leaves right of centre (171.1, beside 'invalid' at 185.1) and then sweeps left across the box top.
verified.root_cause: (1) scene.rs:3347-3370 edge_points back-edge branch returns `[p0, (bt, p0.1 - 40.0), (bt, p3.1 + 40.0), p3]`. The controls move a fixed 40 along the layer axis while bt sits about 170 units out sideways, so both end tangents are nearly horizontal over a 585-unit span. (2) scene.rs:3293 anchor() biases each end toward the OTHER end's centre (`(other.0 - p.b) * 0.35`), not toward the side the bow is on. On Idle this gives 218.3-21.6=196.7. On Rejected the port is pulled right, and ports::assign (ports.rs:355, PORT_SPACING=14 at ports.rs:23) then packs retry exactly 14 units from 'invalid' (171.1 vs 185.1). (3) layout.rs:1368-1376 gives back-edges no dummy channel, so this single-cubic fallback is the only geometry they ever get.
verified.fix_sketch: In the back-edge branch, anchor both ends toward the bow side: call anchor() with `other=(bt, ...)` so the port sits on the half facing the bow. Then emit waypoints instead of a single cubic: p0, then (p0.0, p0.1-d), (bt, p0.1-d-r), (bt, p3.1+d+r), (p3.0, p3.1+d), then p3, with d of about 12-16. The existing spline/waypoint path will then draw the ends as vertical stubs and the arrowhead will meet the border perpendicularly. Alternatively, keep a single cubic but put the controls at (p0.0, p0.1-k) and (p3.0, p3.1+k) with k proportional to |bt-p0.0|; that loses the apex clearance, though.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Routes retry orthogonally up the right side. It leaves the top of Rejected and enters the bottom of Idle along vertical segments.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Draws one 585-unit cubic whose end arrives at 13 degrees, so the arrowhead pokes about 2 units into Idle. It leaves Rejected right of centre, 14 units from 'invalid', and then sweeps left across the box.

The entry port is pushed deliberately past the 'Validating' title chip, which ends at 223.0, plus CHIP_SEP. When a frame's top side lies in a title chip's shadow (CHIP_SHADE), the usable port range is cut to the part past the chip (chip end 223.0 + CHIP_SEP, giving 229.1). The source end on Idle stays at 218.3, and the edge is redrawn as a vertical-tangent cubic, which makes the S. The label placer (labels::relabel) offsets the pill sideways but does not account for the 11-unit drift.

Idle is 131 wide, so 229.1 is well inside it. The edge then stays straight and the label sits cleanly beside or on it. verified.reasoning: The four branch paths each move sideways 21.5 units between vertical-tangent controls (for example 262.1 to 240.6). The zoomed crop shows four wobbly sigmoids. Persist and Notify are centred at 219.3 and 340.9, a span of 121.6, while the bar is only 60 wide.

(b) Give ForkBar its own anchor() arm that puts the port at `other.0` clamped inside the bar, and use bias 0 on the state end when the bar covers that breadth. The branches then become straight verticals, as in a UML fork.

It is a general defect: every TB subgraph gets CLUSTER_HEADER (26) of dead space between its first and second rows, because layout.rs:1495 doubles the header slot symmetrically around the node. Reproduced with no labels: `flowchart TB; subgraph s; A-->B-->C; end` gives A at 68-106, B at 192-230 (gap 86) and C at 290 (gap 60) (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/rev/gap.mmd).

Node titles use labels ('waiting for input') while edge titles use ids ('Rejected → Idle', 'decide → forked'), so the edge title 'decide → Rejected' names a node that has no tooltip anywhere in the SVG. name: sequence
diagram_type: sequence
overall_verdict: For this diagram flowmaid is not ugly next to mermaid. It is more compact (759x962 vs 1060x1391), its frames line up as clean full-width bands, and its inline bold autonumbers read better than mermaid's black circles, which cover the lifelines. What makes it look cheaper is a set of precision bugs plus heavy header styling. Message arrows ignore activation bars: tips run into the bar and lines start at the bar's center. An explicit `activate` bar starts 14px below the message that opens it. A note declared inside `alt` hangs half outside the frame. The notes use the same amber as the API Gateway header and its activation bars. The headers are solid saturated blocks with low-contrast white bold text, and the actor is a pale outlined box instead of a stick figure. There are no mirrored footer participants, so the lifelines just stop below the last frame.
flowmaid_better: Much more compact: viewBox 759x962 vs mermaid 1060x1391 (about half the area) with no loss of content. The participant boxes are sized to their labels (80-109px wide, 34 tall) instead of mermaid's fixed 150x65 boxes.

Autonumbering as a bold '1. ' prefix inside the label (<tspan font-weight=bold>) is cleaner than mermaid's dark numbered circles. Those circles sit on top of lifelines and activation bars and cover arrow starts (mermaid circles 3, 5, 7 overlap the orange activation bar).

Frames are stacked full-width bands (all x=48.9, w=592.6) with a steady 16px gap between them. Mermaid's alt/opt/loop/par boxes all have different widths and x offsets and nearly touch (loop bottom about 1468 vs par top about 1482 in PNG px), so they look scattered.

Frame condition text is not drawn on top of the frame's own top border the way mermaid's is. Mermaid centers '[session valid]', '[every 30s]' and '[slow network]' right under the dotted top edge, and a lifeline runs through them. flowmaid puts the condition next to a filled 'alt'/'opt' chip, which reads well.

The self-message drops the inline '%% self-message'. Mermaid prints 'show spinner %% self-message' literally, and that text runs past the opt frame's left edge (mermaid PNG x about 455 vs frame left about 458). flowmaid's '9. show spinner' sits neatly right of the loop. This is cleaner, but it does differ from mermaid's literal parsing.
Message labels sit 10px above the line, are centered on the span and never touch strokes. Mermaid's 'rows' and 'SELECT widgets' labels have a sequence circle right next to their line ends.
No drop shadows. Lighter frame borders (#aeb6d8, 1.2px solid, rx=4) give a calmer page than mermaid's 2px black dotted frames.

verified.title: Message endpoints use the lifeline center, not the activation bar edge
verified.reasoning: In the flowmaid SVG every API endpoint is x=443.0, the center of the 8px bar (439-447). In the zoomed crop, the msg 2 and msg 6 filled heads run 4px into the bar and cover its stroke, and msg 5 starts at the bar's center and crosses its right half. Bars are emitted before messages (seq.rs:529-539, messages at 602+), so lines and heads paint on top of the white bar. One part of the claim overstates mermaid. Mermaid's leftward outgoing msgs 3 and 7 also start inside the bar (x1=476, bar 470-480), but those rows are exactly where the bar ends, so it does not show. Mermaid does pull incoming arrows back (msg 2 x2=464, msg 6 x2=486) and starts the rightward msg 5 past the bar's right edge (486). flowmaid does none of this.
verified.root_cause: src/seq.rs:322 `let (x0, x1) = (x[*from], x[*to]);` builds the endpoints from column centers only and never looks at the open activation stack `act`. This holds even though the `+` bar is pushed just before (line 324) and the `-` bar is closed just after (line 338). Self-messages (seq.rs:296-312) also start at `cx = x[*from]` whatever the bar state. end_bar (seq.rs:177-186) offsets nested bars by 3px per depth, so center-based endpoints are also wrong for nested bars.
verified.fix_sketch: Add a helper `edge(p, toward_x) -> f64` that returns x[p] when act[p] is empty, and otherwise the bar's center (x[p] + (depth-1)*3) plus or minus ACT_W/2 on the side facing the other end. Call it after the `activate` push for `to`, and before `end_bar` for `from`, so `->>+` and `-->>-` both land on the bar edge. For an explicit `activate` that follows a message to the same participant (needed once explicit-activate-offset is fixed), move the previous message's last point back to the bar edge when processing SeqItem::Activate. Self-messages should start and end at the bar's right edge. Add tests that check head tip x == bar left edge.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Incoming arrows stop at the bar's outer edge, and a rightward outgoing message starts beyond the bar's right edge (msg 5 x1=486, bar 470-480).
verified.what_flowmaid_does: All endpoints sit at the lifeline center (443.0). Heads go 4px into the bar, and msg 5 starts in the middle of the bar.

verified.title: Explicit activate/deactivate bar starts 14px below its message and ends 14px past the last one
verified.reasoning: Reproduced from the code. Msg 4 has cur=272, ly=cur+22=294, then cur+=34 gives 306, and `activate API` pushes cur+2=308. The bar rect starts at y=308 while msg 4 is at y=294. Msg 7 ly=432 gives cur=444, and `deactivate` ends the bar at 446. The zoomed crop shows GET /widgets ending on a bare dashed lifeline, then a gap, then the bar. Mermaid starts the bar exactly at msg 4 (rect y=388 == line y=388) and ends it at msg 7 (388+179=567 == msg 7 y). The shorthand form (160-194) is exact, so the two forms disagree.
verified.root_cause: src/seq.rs:364-365 `SeqItem::Activate(p) => act[*p].push(cur + 2.0)` and `SeqItem::Deactivate(p) => end_bar(..., cur + 2.0, ..)`. `cur` has already moved past the row of the message these statements belong to (cur += ROW_H at line 340, cur += SELF_H + 24 at line 314).
verified.fix_sketch: Keep `last_msg_y: Option<f64>`. Set it to `ly` (or `y1` for a self-message) when a message is emitted, and clear it when a Note, FrameStart, FrameElse or FrameEnd advances `cur`. Activate/Deactivate then use `last_msg_y.unwrap_or(cur + 2.0)`. With the end_bar minimum height of 6 already in place, `activate` immediately followed by `deactivate` still shows. Add a test that compares the bar y0 with the preceding message y.
verified.what_mermaid_does: The bar starts at the y of the message just before `activate` and ends at the y of the message just before `deactivate`.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The bar starts at 308 (msg 4 is at 294) and ends at 446 (msg 7 is at 432): one partial row late at both ends.

verified.title: Note declared inside the alt block sits half outside the alt frame
verified.reasoning: The SVG has the alt rect's right edge at 641.5 and the note at 599.5-734.5, so 93px of the note sits outside. The zoomed crop shows the frame border running behind the note: the frame is drawn first and is visible above and below the card. Mermaid's alt frame is x 64-860 and contains its note at 700-850. A test (rv/t1.mmd) shows the same thing on the left side: `Note left of A` inside nested loop/opt gives a note at x=24-160 while the frames start at 118/128. So this affects any right-of or left-of note on an outer participant.

Notes (seq.rs:341-362) never feed back into frame extents. The normalisation pass (seq.rs:420-450) widens the canvas for the note but not the frame.
verified.fix_sketch: After the row loop, for each frame, grow f.x/f.w to contain every note (and self-message label) whose y falls in [f.y, f.y+f.h], with FRAME_MARGIN. Then walk from outer to inner so each parent still contains its children plus the 10px inset. If the uniform full-width bands should stay, take the min/max over all in-frame notes first and use that as a global frame_l/frame_r. Note x depends only on x[], so a pre-pass works.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Widens the alt frame to x=860 so the 'indexed by tenant' note (700-850) is inside it.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: The frame is fixed at the DB box edge plus 10 (641.5). The note runs to 734.5 and the frame border cuts through it.

verified.title: Notes use the same amber as the third participant (API Gateway) header and activation bars
verified.reasoning: NOTE_STROKE is '#d99114', which equals ACCENTS[2]. The API header fill, the API activation strokes and all four note strokes are #d99114, and the note fill #fcf2da is a tint of the same hue. 'rate-limited', which sits on API's lifeline below the amber bars, reads as API-owned. This is systematic: participant index 2 (and 10, 18, ...) always collides. verified.root_cause: src/seq.rs:37-38 `NOTE_FILL = "#fcf2da"`, `NOTE_STROKE = "#d99114"`, while src/style.rs:87 ACCENTS[2] = "#d99114" is assigned per participant index at seq.rs:654 (`crate::style::accent(i)`) and used for activation strokes at seq.rs:537.

Bold 13px does not count as large text (that needs 18.66px bold), so 4.5:1 applies and all three fail. 'API Gateway' is the hardest label to read in the PNG. This is a deliberate theme choice rather than a geometry bug, so I rate it 1 rather than 2.

verified.what_flowmaid_does: Solid green, amber and pink fills with white bold 13px text (2.6 to 4.1:1).

verified.reasoning: The gaps are 140 / 204.1 / 148.5. Solving 32 + w + 16 + 109.3/2 = 204.1 gives w = 101.45, which is label_width('9. show spinner'), so the self-message rule is what sets this gap. The base gap would be 137.3 and the widest FE-API message label needs about 140. The label ends near x=380, about 63px short of the API lifeline. At that row only the thin lifeline (and at most an 8px bar) exists, so roughly 45-50px is wasted. A test (rv/t1.mmd) shows it in general: A->B gap 200 vs B->C 120 because of one self-message on A.

verified.fix_sketch: Replace `bw[*from + 1] / 2.0` with the real obstacle at that row: ACT_W/2 plus a nested-bar allowance (for example 3*max_depth) plus about 8px. Keep the base `bw/2 + bw/2 + GAP_MIN` floor, which already prevents header overlap.

The 5x crop shows the dashes ending about 4px right of the Visitor lifeline. Arrows with heads hide this because the head covers the end. Mermaid also stops a few px short (x2=79). Low severity.

This is a deliberate trade-off (tidy bands) rather than a bug, but it loses the UML covered-lifelines information. It also causes note-straddles-frame, since frame width never depends on content.

Not visible in this corpus diagram because the API bar ends at 446, before the divider at 454. Fix: emit bars after dividers (S).

A `Note left of <first participant>` inside a frame is never contained, because the left-of gap rule (seq.rs:247-251) only applies when a > 0. In rv/t1.mmd the note is at x=24-160 while the nested loop/opt frames start at 118.1/128.1. The same post-pass fix covers both sides.

The self-message gap inflation is not specific to this diagram. In rv/t1.mmd, a single self-message `A->>A: think hard about it` makes the A->B gap 200 against B->C 120, purely from the `bw[from+1]/2` term at seq.rs:228.

Parity divergence that the first pass listed under flowmaid_better: the sequence parser strips a trailing `%% ...` from message text (src/parser.rs:3362-3367, find_unquoted(line, "%%")). Mermaid 12.2 only treats whole-line `%%` as a comment and renders 'show spinner %% self-message' literally. flowmaid's output is cleaner, but it silently drops user text that mermaid shows (low severity, worth a documented-divergence note).

name: pie
diagram_type: pie
overall_verdict: Flowmaid's pie is not uglier than mermaid's. Its saturated palette, thin white separators, rounded legend swatches and title centred over the whole chart look more modern than mermaid's pastel and lime fills with heavy black outlines. It loses on three things you can see. The thin-slice percentage labels are squeezed into wedges that are too narrow, because the pie is small (r=110 vs 185) and the labels sit close to the centre (0.62r vs 0.75r), so "5%4%" runs together and "4%" sits on the white separator lines. White bold 13px text on orange, green and teal is low contrast. The 0.35% "Trace elements" slice shows up as a hairline seam rather than a slice. Overall it is about 0.65x mermaid's size, so all text is 13px.
flowmaid_better: Categorical palette: #5b6dc0, #33a35c, #d99114, #c2588c, #199a8e and #8a5cd6 are all distinct and visible on white. Mermaid's two biggest slices are near-white (Calcium #ECECFF, Potassium #ffffde, drawn at 0.7 opacity), so their legend swatches almost disappear and the slices are told apart only by black outlines. Its lime (hsl(80,100%,56%)) and yellow (hsl(60,100%,64%)) are garish next to them.
Slice separators are 1.5px white with no outer ring, which looks cleaner than mermaid's 2px black slice strokes plus a 2px black outer circle (r=186).

The title is centred over the whole chart (x=219.4 in a 439-wide canvas). Mermaid centres it over the pie only (x=0 at the pie centre, 225), so it sits left-heavy. Mermaid's 25px title also has about 7px of room at the top (y=-200 relative to a centre at 225, viewBox top at 0).
The legend breathes: 12px rounded swatches (rx=2), an 8px gap from swatch to text, and a 24px row pitch. Mermaid uses 18px square swatches with a 4px gap and a 22px pitch, so text crowds the swatch.

It keeps the tiny 'Trace elements' (0.4) slice in the pie. Mermaid's renderer filters slices under 1% out of the geometry (createPieArcs: filter(value/sum*100 >= 1)) but keeps the legend row, so the legend lists a colour that appears nowhere in the pie.
Margins are balanced (about 20px left and bottom, 26px right, 31px above the title), and the legend is vertically centred on the pie centre (rows 98-230, centre 164 = cy 164).
The SVG is self-contained: explicit width/height, a background rect and inline attributes, with no 4KB embedded stylesheet. It renders the same without CSS.

verified.title: The '4%' label overflows the Zinc wedge and sits on the white separators; '5%4%' reads as one string
verified.reasoning: I re-rendered the flowmaid SVG at 10x with playwright (crop x82-134, y84-112). The '4%' (bold 13px, about 18.8px wide, centred at 119.2,96.7) crosses the Iron/Zinc white separator with its '4' and runs into the Zinc/Trace separator with its '%'. The Zinc wedge (4.37%, 15.7°) is only 18.7px wide at 0.62r = 68.2px. One detail of the first pass is wrong: '5%' does not touch either separator. It clears them by about 1-3px; it is cramped but not overflowing. The main defect holds anyway. The gap between '5%' and '4%' is about 1.3px, and the white separator between them is the same colour as the glyphs, so at 1x they read as '5%4%'. I checked fit geometrically (text box corners against both radial edges, with 1.75px of stroke clearance). At R=110, '4%' only fits from 0.85r outward. At R=130 it fits from 0.70r. Mermaid places labels at 0.75 x 185 = 138.7px (confirmed in its SVG: the 4% label sits at distance 138.7), and its regular 17px text fits there.
verified.root_cause: src/pie.rs:252-265: the label loop puts every slice with frac >= MIN_LABEL_FRAC at the fixed radius ps.r*LABEL_R on the bisector and never compares the text box to the wedge. The constants behind it are src/pie.rs:30 (LABEL_R = 0.62, close to the centre where wedges are narrow), src/pie.rs:18 (RADIUS = 110, small next to bold 13px text: r/font is 8.5, mermaid's is 10.9) and src/pie.rs:33 (MIN_LABEL_FRAC = 0.04, a fixed fraction used as a stand-in for 'fits').
verified.fix_sketch: Option S: set LABEL_R to about 0.72 and RADIUS to about 130. My geometry check shows both '4%' and '5%' then fit with stroke clearance. Option M (better): replace the MIN_LABEL_FRAC gate with a fit test. Compute w = text_width(pct)*13/TEXT_CALIBRATION*1.06 (bold) and h ≈ 10. Step d from LABEL_R*r to 0.86*r in 2px steps and stop at the first d where all four box corners lie at least (stroke/2 + 1px) inside both radial edges and inside the rim. If nothing fits, either skip the label (the legend still carries it, with the value under showData) or put it outside at r+10 with a short leader line, which means scene() must reserve left and top margin. The fit test also brings back labels for 1-4% slices that fit, which is closer to mermaid's ≥1% rule. pie_showcase_parses_and_renders still expects 5 labels for this input.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Regular 17px labels at 0.75 x r185 = 138.7px from the centre. Zinc and Iron labels sit inside their wedges with room to spare. Every slice ≥ 1% gets a label, with no fit check.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Bold 13px labels at a fixed 0.62 x r110 = 68.2px. '4%' is wider than its 18.7px wedge chord and sits on the white separators. '5%' just fits, and its 1.3px gap to '4%' makes the pair read as '5%4%'.

verified.title: Hard-coded white percentage labels fail WCAG AA on 4 of the 5 labelled slices
verified.reasoning: I recomputed WCAG contrast for white text. The first pass's figures are right: #d99114 2.62:1, #33a35c 3.21:1, #199a8e 3.47:1, #5b6dc0 4.78:1. It left out the rose Iron slice #c2588c, which is 4.14:1 and also fails AA for 13px bold (non-large) text. It also counted the violet as passing (4.58:1), but the violet Trace slice has no label. So only 1 of the 5 visible labels (38% on indigo) passes AA, not 2. Mermaid's #333 on its fills blended at 0.7 opacity gives 8.4 to 12.5:1, which confirms that side. Visually '9%' on amber is the weakest.
verified.root_cause: src/pie.rs:258-260 writes fill="#ffffff" for every percentage label whatever the slice colour. The fills come from crate::style::accent (src/style.rs:84-93, ACCENTS), which are mid-luminance colours, so neither white nor dark text works for all of them.
verified.fix_sketch: Add a relative_luminance(hex) and contrast(a,b) helper to style.rs. Per slice, pick whichever of #ffffff and a near-black (#111827) gives the higher contrast against accent(i). That gives indigo with white 4.78, green with dark 6.53, amber 8.01, rose 5.07, teal 6.05 and coral 5.9, all passing AA. Do not use TEXT_COLOR #232840: it only reaches 3.5:1 on rose and 3.0:1 on indigo. Add a unit test that asserts contrast ≥ 4.5 for every ACCENTS entry.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Dark #333 17px text on pastel fills at 0.7 opacity, at 8.4 to 12.5:1 contrast.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: White bold 13px text on every fill: amber 2.62, green 3.21, teal 3.47, rose 4.14, indigo 4.78. Four of the five visible labels fail AA 4.5:1.

verified.title: Pie radius 110 is small compared with its label text (the canvas is about 0.66x mermaid's)
verified.reasoning: The numbers check out: canvas 439x294 vs viewBox 666x450, r 110 vs 185, text 13 vs 17px, title 16 bold vs 25. The 13px body size is flowmaid's house size across diagram types (svg_open is called with 13 / FONT everywhere), so overall scale on its own is a style choice, not a defect. The real problem is the radius relative to the text, and it shows up only as the thin-slice label crowding in issue 1. I would fold this into that issue rather than treat it separately.
verified.root_cause: src/pie.rs:18 RADIUS = 110.0 is a fixed constant that does not depend on label font size or slice count. The base font is set at src/pie.rs:190 (svg_open(..., 13, ...)).
verified.fix_sketch: Raise RADIUS to about 130-140 and keep the 13px text. That brings r/font close to mermaid's ratio and widens every wedge chord by about 20-27%. Canvas height grows by 40-60px. The tests use relative assertions, so none should break apart from any golden snapshots.
verified.what_mermaid_does: r = 185, 17px labels and legend, 25px title, 666x450 viewBox.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: r = 110, 13px bold labels, 13px legend, 16px bold title, 439x294 canvas.

verified.title: The 0.35% 'Trace elements' wedge shows only as a ~0.9px purple line between two white strokes
verified.reasoning: A 12x playwright crop at 12 o'clock shows teal, then a white stroke, a very thin violet strip, another white stroke, then indigo. The strip tapers to nothing toward the centre. Arithmetic: 1.26° at r = 110 is a 2.42px arc, and the violet path's own 1.5px white stroke takes 0.75px from each side (violet is drawn last, so its stroke is on top), leaving about 0.9px at the rim. It looks like a rendering seam, not a data slice. The last slice also touches slice 0 at 12 o'clock, so violet sits next to indigo, the closest hue in the palette. On mermaid: createPieArcs (pieDiagram chunk, line 139) filters out slices under 1% and re-normalises the angles over the remaining slices, while the legend keeps the light-green row. The first pass described that correctly.
verified.root_cause: src/pie.rs:214-249: every non-zero slice is drawn as a wedge with its true sweep, plus stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="1.5" (src/pie.rs:237). There is no minimum visible sweep, and the stroke is not reduced for wedges narrower than about 3x the stroke width.
verified.fix_sketch: In the slice loop, compute rim_len = frac*TAU*r. If rim_len is under about 4px, (a) draw the wedge at a minimum visual sweep of about 2.5° (about 4.8px at r = 110), taking the extra angle from the largest slice (labels and legend keep the true frac), and (b) set stroke-width to min(1.5, rim_len/4) for that wedge. Alternatively, draw the fills without strokes, then draw the white radial separators in a second pass and leave out the separator on the far side of a tiny slice. Changing the palette order or the colour of the last slice when it would sit next to slice 0 would also help.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Leaves <1% slices out of the pie geometry and the labels, re-normalises the other angles, and keeps the legend row, so the legend shows a colour that appears nowhere in the pie.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Draws a true 1.26° wedge whose own 1.5px white stroke leaves about 0.9px of violet at the rim, next to similar indigo. It is barely findable.

verified.title: <title>/aria-label are hard-coded to 'Pie chart'; the declared title, and even explicit accTitle/accDescr, are dropped
verified.reasoning: pie.flowmaid.svg has role=img aria-label="Pie chart" and <title>Pie chart</title>, although the source declares 'title Key elements in Product X'. I also tested more than the first pass did. A pie with 'accTitle: My acc' and 'accDescr: desc' still renders aria-label="Pie chart" with no <desc>, so explicit accessibility statements are parsed and then discarded. Mermaid honours accTitle/accDescr for pie through its common a11y path. It does not use the plain title as the accessible name either, so the plain-title part is not a regression against mermaid, but losing accTitle is.
verified.root_cause: src/pie.rs:190 passes the literal string "Pie chart" to svg_open. src/parser.rs:3785-3788: parse_pie calls extract_acc and binds the result to `_acc`, then drops it on purpose (the comment says new public fields would break struct-literal users). src/model.rs:1024 PieChart has no acc_title/acc_descr fields, so render.rs:70 render_pie_with has nothing to pass on. Class and ER already use svg_open_a11y with A11y (class.rs:200, er.rs:191).
verified.fix_sketch: S: in to_svg_with, use ps.title.as_deref().unwrap_or("Pie chart") as the accessible name. M: carry acc_title/acc_descr through. Either add the fields to PieChart (with Default, at a minor version bump, or #[non_exhaustive]) or return them next to the model, then add pie::to_svg_a11y_with(ps, &A11y, opts) that calls svg_open_a11y, the way class.rs and er.rs do. Precedence: accTitle, then title, then 'Pie chart'.
verified.what_mermaid_does: aria-roledescription="pie". accTitle/accDescr become <title>/<desc>. The plain `title` is not used as the accessible name.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Always aria-label/<title> 'Pie chart'. accTitle/accDescr are parsed and silently discarded.

missed: The legend width is mis-measured, so the right margin is too wide (visible, low severity). This also refutes the first pass's 'balanced margins, 26px right' praise. The PNG is a 1.5x render with an 8px body margin, so 12px offset. Measured in SVG units, content spans x 20.7 to 404.7 in the 439-wide canvas: 20px on the left and about 34px on the right (top about 30, bottom about 21). Root cause: src/pie.rs:126 sizes the legend column with layout::text_width, which is calibrated at 14px (src/layout.rs:173 TEXT_CALIBRATION = 14.0), but the legend is drawn at 13px and the result is never scaled by 13/14. text_width('Trace elements [0.4]') = 131 against an actual 116.7px. src/pie.rs:145 scales the title by 16.0/13.0 when it should be 16.0/TEXT_CALIBRATION, and it ignores the 1.06 bold factor; those two errors roughly cancel here. Fix (S): multiply by 13.0/TEXT_CALIBRATION at pie.rs:126, and use *16.0/TEXT_CALIBRATION*1.06 at pie.rs:145.

Explicit accTitle/accDescr in a pie are parsed and thrown away (src/parser.rs:3785-3788 binds the result to `_acc`). I verified it: 'accTitle: My acc' still yields aria-label="Pie chart" and no <desc>. That is a real regression against mermaid, which emits <title>/<desc>, and goes further than the first pass's 'generic name' note. I folded it into generic-accessible-name above.

Latent, not visible in this 6-slice render: the pie palette is the shared 8-entry ACCENTS list (src/style.rs:84-93, accent() wraps at 8). With 9 slices, slice 8 gets #5b6dc0, the same as slice 0, and the last slice always touches slice 0 at 12 o'clock. I verified this with a 9-equal-slice pie: the two wedges merge into one indigo area, separated only by a white stroke, and two legend rows share a colour. Mermaid cycles 12 pie colours (pie1 to pie12). Fix (S): a dedicated pie palette of 12 or more, or skip any colour equal to slice 0's for the last slice.

Latent: percentage text uses Rust `{:.0}` (src/pie.rs:260), which rounds exact ties half-to-even, while mermaid uses JS toFixed(0). I verified with values 1 and 7: flowmaid prints '12%', mermaid prints '13%'. Also, MIN_LABEL_FRAC = 0.04 (src/pie.rs:33) hides labels that mermaid shows for 1-3.99% slices: a 3.9% slice gets no label in flowmaid, while mermaid prints '4%'. Not triggered by this input. Fix (S): round with (x*100.0 + 0.5).floor() for non-negative values, and gate labels on the geometric fit test from the thin-slice fix instead of on 4%.

name: mindmap
diagram_type: mindmap
overall_verdict: Flowmaid's palette is calmer and more consistent than mermaid's neon one, and its labels never wrap awkwardly. As a mind map it still looks worse, mainly because of the layout. Every depth sits on a fixed ring around the root (RING=172), so the result is a sparse, nearly square spider web: small 32px chips hang off long, thin spokes of uneven length, and only 9% of the canvas has ink, against 31% for mermaid. On top of that the root is a pale grey-lavender ellipse that recedes behind its own children, the edge taper is too weak to show hierarchy, and the cloud, bang, default and rounded shapes are hard or impossible to tell apart.
flowmaid_better: Calmer, coherent 4-hue branch palette (#5b6dc0 / #33a35c / #d99114 / #c2588c) instead of mermaid's neon yellow #ffff78, lime, magenta #ff86ff and near-pure #0000ec root; it looks more professional
Long labels stay on one line in tidy pills. Mermaid force-wraps 'YAML frontmatter', 'Orthogonal routing' and 'Interactive scene' into bulky 150x78 two-line boxes with awkward breaks

No mismatched underline glitch. Mermaid draws a complementary-colored bar under default nodes (lavender under yellow 'Input', green under magenta 'Reach'/'CLI'/'Web'), which reads like a rendering artifact

Predictable, balanced radial order: the root is centered (475,385 in a 909x773 canvas), branches run clockwise from 12 o'clock in source order (Input, Engine, Output, Reach), and margins are an even 28px on all sides. Mermaid's force layout places branches arbitrarily (Input ends up lower-right, Output upper-left)
No edge crossings and no node crowding anywhere
Pure SVG <text> with no <foreignObject>, so it renders in non-browser viewers. File is 6.9 KB vs mermaid's 49 KB
The bang is drawn as a starburst, which arguably reads more like an 'explosion' than mermaid's scalloped badge

verified.title: Sparse, oversized, near-square canvas with large dead zones
verified.reasoning: I re-measured this. The viewBoxes are 909x773 (flowmaid) and 809.6x489.6 (mermaid), so flowmaid's canvas is 1.77x the area. Non-white pixel fraction on my own count is 0.093 vs 0.302. One nuance the first pass missed: mermaid's summed node area is also 1.75x flowmaid's (120k vs 68.5k px², from 16px text, 20px padding and wrapped 150x78 boxes). So the sparse look comes about half from the spread-out layout and half from the small nodes (see undersized-chips). The layout half is the bigger lever. I built a scratch copy with RING=120 and tangent-projected footprints, and the canvas dropped to 715x564 (-43% area, about mermaid's 397k px²) with no overlaps on this input.
verified.root_cause: src/mindmap.rs:28 RING=172.0 and :180 (rad[k] = RING*k): fixed ring radii that ignore node sizes, so the root->branch distance is always 172 centre to centre, about 100-127px of visible trunk. src/mindmap.rs:107-112, :175 and :184 size each node's angular footprint from its full box diagonal (hypot(w,h)), whatever side of the ring the node is on. A 140x32 leaf on the left or right of the ring is charged 140px of arc when it really needs about 32px. That inflates the depth-2 ring: with diagonals it needs r>=299 (the actual 344 comes from RING*2); with tangent-projected extents it needs only about 227. place() (:137-157) then spreads the whole 2π (:197) over those rings, so the bounding box is about 2*344 plus half box widths in every direction.
verified.fix_sketch: (1) Derive the depth-1 radius from content instead of RING: root_half + max child half-extent + about 60px. (2) Replace the diagonal footprint with the box extent projected onto the ring tangent, |w*sin φ| + |h*cos φ| + pad, and run 2-3 refinement passes (allocate, read the angles, recompute footprints, regrow the rings). (3) Keep a radial separation guard, rad[k] >= rad[k-1] + half-extents + gap. I prototyped this in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/fm (output /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-flowmaid/cac93b13-7009-5470-94b5-477c61df0333/scratchpad/exp1.png), and it produced a 715x564 canvas. Full parity with mermaid's density needs the parent-centric placement described under uneven-long-leaf-spokes.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Uses a 909x773 canvas, about 9% ink: concentric rings at r=172 and r=344 around the root.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Uses an 810x490 canvas, about 30% ink, from the cose-bilkent force layout (mindmap-definition chunk, line 1000: layout = "cose-bilkent").

verified.title: Leaf spokes are long and uneven, often longer than the trunk edges (spider look)
verified.reasoning: I computed visible lengths (border to border) from the SVG. Flowmaid leaves: Reach->Eleven 54.8, Engine->Ortho 72.4, Output->Zero 76.8, ... Output->SVG 190.3, Engine->Layered 196.8, Reach->Web 210.1, Engine->Hit-testing 222.6. Flowmaid trunks: 99-127. Mermaid's visible edges, measured the same way, all fall in 49-82. The spread in flowmaid is about 4x, against about 1.7x in mermaid. My tightened-ring prototype shrank the canvas but kept the unevenness (19-127px), which shows this needs its own fix.
verified.root_cause: src/mindmap.rs:152-153: c[k] = (r*cos(mid), r*sin(mid)) with r = rad[depth], measured from the ROOT, not the parent. :145-150 hands each child a share of the parent's whole wedge. Engine's wedge is about 112°, so the leaves at its edges sit about 42° off Engine's direction. Their distance from Engine is sqrt(172² + 344² - 2·172·344·cos42°) ≈ 245 centre to centre, while the leaf nearest Engine's direction is only 172 + 3 centre to centre.
verified.fix_sketch: Use parent-centric placement. For each child, set its distance from the PARENT to parent_half + child_half (along the direction) + L, with L≈55. Choose its angle inside the wedge as seen from the parent, allowing up to about 150° facing outward, then resolve collisions with a sweep or a few iterations of box-repulsion relaxation. The alternative is a short force-directed relaxation (spring rest length = half-sizes + L, rectangle repulsion) seeded from the current radial result, which keeps the deterministic order. Add a test that bounds max/min visible edge length.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Leaves sit on a global depth-2 ring, so visible spokes run 55-223px.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Leaves cluster around their parent, so visible edges run 49-82px.

verified.title: Root node is the faintest element; it does not read as the focal point
verified.reasoning: #c9cfe0 has 1.56:1 contrast against white (I recomputed this). Every other node is a saturated accent. The root is 80x50 against 32px-tall chips and uses 14px bold text, the same size as everything else. In the PNG the eye lands on the coloured branches before the centre. Mermaid's root is an 88px #0000ec circle (9.5:1 against white). The text itself is readable (9.3:1 on the fill), so the problem is visual weight, not legibility.
verified.root_cause: src/mindmap.rs:38-39: ROOT_FILL = "#c9cfe0", ROOT_TEXT = TEXT_COLOR. Applied at :236-237. label_svg (:407-411) only bolds the root and never changes its size. node_size (:93-96) gives the root just base_h*1.6 width.
verified.fix_sketch: Fill the root with a strong neutral, e.g. TEXT_COLOR #232840 or a dark indigo, with white bold text. Give the root a larger font (16-18px) and extra padding. That needs a font-size attribute on the root's <text> and text_width scaled by size/14.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Pale grey-lavender 80x50 ellipse with 14px dark text.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Saturated blue 88px circle with white text.

verified.title: root((flowmaid)) declares a circle but is drawn as a 1.6:1 ellipse
verified.reasoning: The SVG has <ellipse rx=39.9 ry=24.8>. The code deliberately makes height = max(base_h, 0.62·d). Mermaid emits <circle r=43.77>.
verified.root_cause: src/mindmap.rs:93-96: MindShape::Circle => { let d = base_w.max(base_h*1.6); (d, base_h.max(d*0.62)) }. shape_svg (:382-389) then draws an ellipse from w/2 and h/2.
verified.fix_sketch: Return (d, d) with d = max(base_w, base_h) + about 12px. The text sits at the centre, so the label width must stay below about 0.9·d. Optionally emit <circle> when w == h. Only mindmap.rs uses this, so there are no other painters to update. Add a test asserting w == h for Circle.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: 80x50 ellipse.
verified.what_mermaid_does: True circle, r=43.8.

verified.title: Cloud shape is jagged and reads as a second explosion; cloud and bang are hard to tell apart
verified.reasoning: In a zoomed crop, 'Eleven diagram types' is a faceted, saw-toothed blob with 14px horizontal spikes at both ends: the points (30.2,294.9), (44.2,291.7), (30.2,288.5) form a spike only 6px tall. It reads as a torn or jagged badge, not a puffy cloud. Up close it is still less spiky than the 16-point bang, so 'impossible to tell apart' overstates it. But at normal and downscaled sizes both read as explosions, while mermaid's cloud has clearly convex, puffy lobes. The flat 227x49 box (4.6:1 aspect) makes it worse; mermaid's cloud box is about 164x100.
verified.root_cause: src/mindmap.rs:327-339 cloud_pts: steps=48, bumps=9, f = 0.86 + 0.14*|sin(9θ)|. |sin(9θ)| has 18 lobes, so each lobe gets only about 2.7 vertices and becomes a triangle with a sharp cusp in the valley. The points are spaced by parametric angle on a very flat ellipse, and the radial bump scales with rx (0.14·113.6 ≈ 16px), so near θ=0 and θ=π the bumps turn into long horizontal spikes. The sizing at :97 (base_w*1.4+8, base_h*1.35+6) is what makes the shape so flat. The docs at src/model.rs:1132-1135 are stale ('approximated as an ellipse' / 'bold pill').
verified.fix_sketch: Build the cloud from circular arcs. Put k = round(perimeter/32) bump centres evenly by arc length around an inner ellipse, take the outer arc of each, and sample about 8 points per arc so perimeter() still returns a polygon for GUI painters (or emit SVG 'A' arcs in to_svg). Change the sizing to something puffier, e.g. (base_w*1.15+16, max(base_h*1.9, 0.42*w)). Update the model.rs doc comments.
verified.what_flowmaid_does: Jagged 48-vertex |sin| polygon with spiky ends.
verified.what_mermaid_does: Puffy convex-lobed cloud.

verified.title: Default (undelimited) nodes and (rounded) nodes render identically
verified.reasoning: The SVG shows Input and YAML frontmatter both as rx=14 pills. The parser maps undelimited text to Rounded. One option: Default = rx 4 rect with a 2px darker underline, Rounded = rx 14 pill. Update the tests shapes_and_br_parse and multiword_text_before_paren_stays_literal, which currently expect Rounded.
